articles.title: Shopping scams: how to spot them and save money | Kaspersky official blog
articles.context: Cybercriminals use the stolen data both to steal money and to launch follow-up attacks
articles.full_text:
Black Friday is just around the corner — that time of year when a refrigerator that normally sells for $599.99 suddenly becomes a refrigerator that sells for “just $749.99 $599.99!”, online stores start writing in ALL CAPS, and every other website has a countdown timer that somehow knows that in exactly 14 minutes and 37 seconds, your life without a new vacuum cleaner will lose all meaning.

Kaspersky experts have looked at how cybercriminals exploit the Black Friday frenzy to steal users’ money and data. Today, we’re taking a look at this year’s most common scams. You can read the full report on Securelist.

A discount in name only

Let’s start with a classic: fake discounts. In the run-up to Black Friday, crafty sellers raise their prices so they can pass off the regular price as a discounted one. So that refrigerator that’s always cost $599.99 goes on sale on Black Friday for… $599.99. How generous!

Some stores and sellers care so little about their reputation that they simply pass off their regular prices as discounted ones without even raising them beforehand. These “discounts” may come with bold claims like “TODAY ONLY!”, “exclusive offer”, “hurry before it’s gone”, or “only one left in stock”. As you can probably guess, these claims usually have nothing to do with reality — they’re simply designed to trigger shoppers’ FOMO.

These tricks are as old as the hills, but fortunately, checking whether a store is being honest is easy in this case: just enter the product page URL into the Internet Archive and compare prices in the available snapshots from the past few months. If there aren’t any snapshots, try one of the many price history services.

It’s also worth comparing the price of the same product at other stores. This is where AI can come in handy, along with the useful prompts from our post Hacking Black Friday: using LLMs to save on the “sale of the year”.

How to tell scammers from legitimate sellers

If crafty sellers were all we had to worry about, we’d just compare prices and live happily ever after. Unfortunately, Black Friday is that time of year when scams and phishing schemes traditionally surge.

Scam websites are pretty straightforward: the prices are suspiciously low, and shoppers either never receive their orders or end up getting something completely different from what they expected. Phishing sites, on the other hand, impersonate well-known retailers and brands, but their goal is to get their hands not only on your money but also on your sensitive information: your name, address, phone number, payment card details, email address, and much, much more. Cybercriminals use the stolen data both to steal money and to launch follow-up attacks. For example, they might send you a message supposedly from a delivery service (“Your item failed inspection; you’ll need to request a refund”, “Confirm your delivery address”) or even try to impersonate employees of your bank.

Scammers impersonate Spotify and YouTube Premium to steal payment details and account credentials

Some phishing sites go even further, trying to trick users into downloading malware disguised as a retailer’s app, a discount coupon, an “order confirmation” file, or a browser update. A shopping trip gone wrong could leave you not only out of pocket but also with malware on your device.

With AI, cybercriminals can create hundreds or even thousands of these sites, making minor changes to the website address — for example, amazzon instead of amazon. The site’s design, meanwhile, can look virtually identical to the original.

Scammers often copy the fonts and design of legitimate stores. Above is an example of a fake Amazon page

Here’s a checklist to help you vet a store before making a purchase and protect yourself from scams:

Check when the domain was registered. If the online store has only been around for a few months or even days, that’s a major red flag that you might’ve stumbled across a scam.

Take a close look at the prices. Even the most generous discounts have their limits. If you’re being offered goods for next to nothing, someone’s probably trying to scam you.

Look for the store’s registered address — a missing address or an unusual location should raise suspicions.

Read the reviews carefully. Remember, a lack of negative reviews doesn’t guarantee that a store is trustworthy: sellers sometimes artificially inflate their ratings. Still, it’s worth looking — a single negative review might help you make the right decision.

Check the website you’re on. If the online store doesn’t use HTTPS or your browser warns you about a potential threat, don’t buy anything there.

To avoid falling for scammers’ tricks, use Kaspersky Premium. Our security solution detects fake domains and scam websites, blocks access to suspicious sites, and prevents malicious downloads. By the way, Kaspersky Premium also works with email, alerting you to phishing and spam. And from Black Friday until New Year’s, you can get it at up to 45% off* — for real, we promise!

AI scams: how to avoid buying AI-generated products

You might’ve seen one of the many viral videos in which a well-known clothing brand supposedly unveils adorable hoodies with a special pocket for pets. We hate to break it to you, but most of these videos are AI-generated, and the brand has never sold any such hoodies.

Over the past few years, savvy scammers have been making money selling products that don’t exist. These days, it’s easy to generate a convincing video of someone trying on nonexistent clothes or reviewing a made-up product. People who order these AI-generated products usually either receive nothing at all or end up with something completely different from what they expected: entirely different items, poor-quality knockoffs, or even… printed photos and miniature versions of the products they bought. And no, we’re not kidding!

Expectation vs. reality: instead of a Christmas decoration, a Reddit user received an image of it printed on a piece of fabric. Source And here, instead of the promised knitted sweater, the shopper received a cheap polyester T-shirt with a sweater printed on it. For $55, no less! Source

These products are mostly advertised on social media and live shopping (live commerce) platforms. Before you follow a link in the description or copy a product code from the comments, check who posted the video: is it a well-known brand? What information can you find about it online — does it have a registered address or an official website? Where exactly is the product being sold?

Don’t trust every influencer you come across, especially if their bio says something like “UGC creator” (user-generated content creator). These creators make money producing promotional content for brands, and a glowing review doesn’t necessarily mean you’ll receive a genuine, high-quality product.

What’s more, some “influencers” are actually entirely AI-generated, and they look pretty realistic. Many platforms actually require AI-generated content to be labeled, but creators don’t always follow the rules. It’s also worth checking when the supposed influencer’s account was created — scam accounts tend to pop up out of nowhere and don’t last long.

But what if you can’t find anything conclusive about the influencer or store? Then it’s time to take a closer look at the product ad itself. Watch out for these red flags:

the product or background looks unrealistic;

unusual highlights and shadows typical of AI-generated content;

people in the video or photo look unnatural, have the wrong number of fingers, or their jewelry, clothing details, and other small features keep changing;

the product itself looks “perfect”, has an unusual structure, or features a fantastical design you’ve never seen anywhere else;

suspiciously low prices.

You can also try a reverse image search for the product. Take a screenshot and upload it to a search engine — sometimes it turns out that the “exclusive designer sweater” has been circulating online for years in a very different form, or that the seller simply took someone else’s photo and tweaked it a little.

A promo code for 100% off your bank balance

Another less obvious type of scam involves bogus promotions and coupons. And no, we’re not talking about how most promo codes only work on your first order — or don’t work at all.

In the run-up to the holidays and major sales, scammers sell special paid “subscriptions” that supposedly give you access to coupons and promo codes for major retailers. Once you’ve paid, you’re promised regular deliveries of promo codes, coupons, or gift cards by mail — except you either receive nothing or get fake coupons that can’t be redeemed. These services are often offered on well-known online marketplaces.

Sometimes, scammers offering coupons promise an extra discount to anyone who completes their purchase on the scammers’ own website. In one case, a seller was offering drones for around $200 less than usual. The shopper paid by card and even received a tracking number, but the shipment status never updated. The seller then claimed they were waiting for payment confirmation, and before long their phone number was disconnected altogether. The shopper never received the drone.

Finally, you might get an email or message urging you to activate a unique coupon worth an eye-watering amount — today only, of course, and preferably within the next ten minutes. To claim this windfall, all you have to do is follow a link and enter all your sensitive information, including your payment card number. Quite a catch for the criminal!

So, if you want real promo codes on Black Friday, sign up for retailers’ own newsletters, check the offers sections on their official websites, and use well-known deal aggregators. But be wary of “exclusive” promotions from random posts and emails.

A box full of empty promises: mystery box scams

Want to buy a new smartphone for next to nothing? How about a game console?

Another popular lure is “mystery boxes” or “return pallets” supposedly filled with customer returns or surplus warehouse stock. For a small sum, sellers promise a whole box of random goods that could supposedly contain smartphones, laptops, headphones, and other expensive electronics. The catch? The contents are often much less impressive than the ads promise.

Last year, in the run-up to Black Friday, there were discovered more than 2,000 fake online stores offering “Amazon returns”. Scammers registered dozens of similar-looking domains, copied the designs of well-known retailers, and promised expensive electronics for next to nothing — in the end, shoppers never got the goods they’d been promised and simply handed their data over to the cybercriminals.

Some major retailers do have programs for selling returned items, but these offers are usually only available to other businesses, not ordinary consumers.

How to save money on Black Friday without getting scammed

Don’t focus solely on the size of the discount. Compare prices at different stores and make sure you check how much the product cost before the sale.

Make sure you’re on the legitimate website. Check how long the site has been around and whether the retailer provides contact details and legal information.

Go directly to the retailer’s website. If you receive a promotional email or find a promo code for a huge discount on social media, find the brand’s official website through a search engine or open the app you normally use instead of following the link you’ve been sent.

Don’t fall for AI-generated content. If an item only exists in a single viral video, look for it on the brand’s official website or try a reverse image search. If the product looks odd or just too unusual, trust your instincts!

Don’t share unnecessary information. A store doesn’t need your card number or home address to give you a discount. And if you have to pay a suspicious fee up front to claim a “gift”, it’s probably no gift at all.

Use a comprehensive security solution. Even the most attentive shopper might miss an extra letter in a website address or a well-disguised phishing email. Kaspersky Premium detects fake domains and scam websites, warns you about suspicious sites, blocks malicious downloads, and helps identify phishing emails. And right now, thanks to Black Friday and holiday discounts, you’ve got over a month to get it at up to 45% off*!

For more on the red flags to watch out for this Black Friday, read our report on Securelist.

And if you want to make the most of Black Friday, check out our post Hacking Black Friday: using LLMs to save on the “sale of the year”. We’ve put together ready-to-use prompts for ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, and other AI assistants to help you:

check whether a store has really lowered its prices or quietly raised them just before the sale;

find cheaper alternatives to a product and compare their specifications;

compare offers from several stores, taking both price and shipping into account;

analyze reviews and identify recurring product issues;

Introduction

Preinstalled malware on mobile devices is a major threat to user security and privacy. When we buy a new smartphone or tablet, we expect it to be ready to use and secure right out of the box. In some cases, however, devices ship with malware already on them. Such malware can do almost anything: display ads, collect personal data and credentials, track user activity, and more. Preinstalled malware can also turn the infected device into a tool for fraud, such as stealing credit card numbers or other sensitive information, causing financial loss and reputational damage.

We’ve previously reported cases where users bought smartphones on marketplaces with malware already preinstalled. Over the past few months, however, several large organizations have encountered malware embedded in the firmware of mobile devices. The specific risks to corporate security depend on how the devices are used and on the company’s line of business. But because the Trojan sits in the device firmware, any app can be compromised, and the potential damage is hard to overstate. This post looks at the current landscape of preinstalled threats on mobile devices, the risks they pose to corporate users, and available countermeasures, including Kaspersky solutions.

Landscape of preinstalled threats

The total number of devices with malicious code found in their firmware or system apps keeps growing. According to Kaspersky Security Network, the number of such devices detected each month has increased more than 2.5-fold over the past year.

Monthly number of Android devices with preinstalled malware detected by Kaspersky solutions, November 2025 — October 2026 (download)

Several malware families are known to spread through firmware and system apps, the most common being Keenadu and Triada. According to our data, one or another of these two families was found on 88% of infected devices in the first ten months of 2026.

The Triada backdoor (Backdoor.AndroidOS.Triada) was discovered ten years ago and has remained popular with attackers ever since. Early versions of the malware actively exploited Android vulnerabilities to gain root access and the privileges they needed. At that time, Triada was often distributed as a regular app. Over time, however, Android introduced tighter restrictions, and attackers now mostly use the preinstalled version of this backdoor. Throughout 2026, users encountered about twenty markedly distinct variants. The most common ones were Backdoor.AndroidOS.Triada.ag and Backdoor.AndroidOS.Triada.z. The latest Triada versions have two key distinguishing features: the ability to inject malicious functionality into any app on the device, system or user-installed, and a modular architecture that lets attackers tailor the malware to their current targets with additional payloads. Known modules can steal credentials for messaging and social media apps, intercept calls and text messages, replace links in browsers, siphon off cryptocurrency, and run a reverse proxy on the infected device. It’s worth stressing that by loading additional modules, attackers get virtually unlimited capabilities.

Keenadu is another preinstalled backdoor we discovered, which appeared relatively recently. The earliest known firmware version that contains this malware dates back to 2023. Even so, the number of devices infected with Keenadu is considerable: according to our data, more than 220,000 devices were infected in the first ten months of 2026.

Keenadu is similar to Triada in many ways, especially in its main architectural feature: once it’s on a device, attackers can download additional modules with any functionality and inject them into target apps. In most known Keenadu attacks, the malware was used for ad fraud, in particular to generate fake clicks. Technically, however, it can perform any action on the infected device. Notably, on first contact with the C2 servers, the backdoor versions we analyzed received a command to activate after about two and a half months. Until then, the malware showed no activity. This is probably meant to give the device owner time to install all the apps they need and settle into daily use, and to make the compromise harder to detect.

Other families of preinstalled malware exist, although they’re less common than Triada and Keenadu. They include Dwphon, Vo1d, and BADBOX. Their functionality is generally similar: mostly ad fraud and traffic redirection. Note that most cases involve phones and tablets, but preinstalled backdoors also threaten other types of devices. For example, Dwphon has turned up in the firmware of children’s smartwatches, and Vo1d samples in TV box firmware.

Corporate environment

We first saw an organization, rather than a home user, encounter preinstalled malware several years ago. That case involved the Dwphon malware. Over the past year, however, we’ve received more and more reports from different customers. In less than a year, several large organizations have come to us with the same request. After installing Kaspersky Endpoint Security for Android on brand-new, out-of-the-box devices, they saw detections of Keenadu or Triada and asked us to confirm that those detections were genuine.

Note that when we talk about corporate threats, we mean the Corporate Owned, Business Only (COBO) and Corporate Owned, Personally Enabled (COPE) usage scenarios, where the employee’s device belongs to the organization. The difference between these models is that COBO doesn’t allow personal use of the device (and usually blocks it at the software level). With COPE, the organization controls global settings but allows free personal use and, in some cases, even installation of third-party apps. By corporate environment, we mean primarily the setup with centralized procurement, where an organization buys all the devices it needs (hundreds, thousands, or even tens of thousands) for uniform use. This post doesn’t cover infections under the Bring Your Own Device (BYOD) model, where employees use infected personal devices they bought themselves to access company resources or for work communications.

Preinstalled malware appears on a new device as a result of a supply chain attack. Devices can be manufactured and flashed in different places. Likewise, different parties in the production process can create the firmware and prepare it for the device. Malicious code typically gets onto a device in one of three ways:

The manufacturer installs the malware deliberately: the attackers control the entire production process and either sell infected devices cheaply under an obscure brand name or, conversely, pose as a well-known manufacturer, damaging that company’s reputation.

A legitimate brand that makes the final device receives malicious firmware from a contractor acting in bad faith.

A legitimate manufacturer builds the firmware in-house, but the build relies on an already infected base or code component. Here, no one directly involved in manufacturing knows the production chain has been compromised.

What risks do corporate customers face when they buy such devices? Based on the technical capabilities of preinstalled malware, we can identify the following main risks:

Degraded performance of infected devices: shorter battery life, overheating, and glitches in various apps. Some devices have even been known to play random sounds on their own.

Ads on devices, both visible to the user and hidden. They consume extra traffic and also connect the device to various websites, which creates a separate group of risks.

Account takeover in messaging apps, social media, and corporate resources: theft of credentials can damage the company’s reputation and lead to financial losses or even new attacks.

Direct financial losses, such as cryptocurrency theft.

Theft of confidential data and secrets: in effect, spying on corporate devices.

Use in a proxy botnet: the organization’s infected devices can relay arbitrary traffic to any internet resources.

Use in a DDoS botnet: infected devices can be enlisted to launch DDoS attacks on any target. Reputational risks come into play here as well.

External access to the corporate infrastructure through a proxy module. Infected devices are known to have been used as residential proxies to infect other devices on the same local network.

Device downtime: attackers who disable corporate devices in active use can disrupt operations.

Note that not all of the attack scenarios involving preinstalled malware listed above have been seen in real-world incidents. However, Triada and BADBOX, for example, have already expanded their functionality: besides displaying ads, they now steal accounts. We can therefore expect preinstalled malware to keep gaining capabilities that pose even higher risks.

Using Kaspersky solutions to mitigate risks

Mobile Device Management (MDM) is a separate category of solutions built to manage mobile devices, and it helps mitigate infection risks in corporate environments. With MDM, IT teams can centrally configure smartphones, tablets and laptops, enforce security policies, and control app installation. This significantly reduces the risk of infection caused by user actions, because it prevents a user from installing an APK from an attacker’s message, a malicious website, or a rogue app store listing.

However, these measures alone are not effective against preinstalled Trojans. Centralized mobile device management alone is not enough to contain threats like Triada and Keenadu. It must be complemented by protection that can detect malware, including any already present on a device before the company starts using it. The best approach is to combine management and protection in a single agent with a unified console, which simplifies rollout and day-to-day operation: IT teams only need to deploy and maintain one application instead of two.

Kaspersky Next product line, starting with Kaspersky Next EDR Optimum, combines Advanced MDM functionality with antivirus protection. The antivirus engine scans files and installed apps and provides real-time protection. Kaspersky Next can detect malware on Android devices, even in preinstalled apps, and alert administrators to any threats it finds. This allows spotting an infection on a device that nominally complies with corporate policies.

Triada detection report in the unified KSC console (screenshot in Russian)

Note that it’s technically impossible for either antivirus tools or the OS itself to remove preinstalled malware from the system partition. However, Kaspersky Next lowers the risk of buying a whole batch of devices and then finding a preinstalled Trojan that is hard or impossible to remove by reflashing. If Kaspersky Next detects malware like Triada or Keenadu, it alerts the IT administrator, who can then contain the threat by blocking the device’s internet access, clearing app data, rotating passwords, or locking the device entirely. Administrators can monitor and manage the infected device from the unified console of the Kaspersky Security Center.

Threat monitoring in the unified KSC console

Companies planning a mobile infrastructure should account for the risk of encountering preinstalled malware. Before ordering a large batch of devices, we recommend inspecting and pilot-testing sample units. We should stress that this measure is no substitute for installing security software on every device used in the organization. Even if the tests come out fine, an unscrupulous supplier may have deliberately sent clean units for inspection. Protection must also be continuous because, for example, the device update system could come under attack.

Manufacturers need to check devices and firmware code for malware just as customers do. Whether the firmware is written in-house or by a contractor, the result can contain malicious code, as we noted earlier. To detect preinstalled threats, you need a file scanning solution that can respond quickly when it finds malware. Kaspersky Scan Engine is one of the Kaspersky products designed for this task. The engine uses the latest detection technologies to identify a wide range of cyberthreats, including preinstalled ones. It integrates easily into a variety of workflows. For example, it can connect to a software build pipeline or any other system that needs to check files for malicious code.

articles.title: Who reads ChatGPT user conversations and views photos in Copilot? | Kaspersky official blog
articles.context: But where does OpenAI get these prompts from in the first place
articles.full_text:
People routinely share personal data with AI chatbots and ask them intimate questions, covering everything from mental and physical health to finances, red tape, sexual fantasies, and plenty more. Many assume these exchanges remain strictly private between user and model.

Yet recent investigations by journalists show that complete privacy is far from guaranteed when interacting with AI. It turns out that the developers of two popular tools — OpenAI’s ChatGPT and Microsoft’s Copilot — hire human staff to read user prompts and check the AI’s responses.

According to information obtained by the journalists, OpenAI relies on meatbags to judge whether its AI responds accurately to text prompts, while Microsoft uses human contractors to check how faithfully its AI generates or edits images based on user requests. Workers interviewed by the journalists say they sometimes review user prompts that have not been anonymized. In this piece, we examine both cases in detail, and explain how to keep your conversations with AI private.

Who’s reading your ChatGPT conversations, how, and why

In mid-September, 404 Media reported on an OpenAI initiative known as Project Lily, through which the company brings in outside contractors to evaluate and improve the quality of its AI’s responses to user prompts. According to 404 Media, a company named Mercor helps hire these reviewers. Remember the name Mercor, because we’ll come back to it.

The journalists got hold of a trove of Project Lily documents: instructions for employees, Slack conversations, real ChatGPT user prompts, and the scoring system reviewers use to rate the chatbot’s responses. Judging by these materials, a chat review can go through several stages.

Read the prompt. The reviewer selects a task in a dedicated system and is presented with a real user’s ChatGPT prompt. At times, the prompt is accompanied by the chat history and a brief profile of the user compiled from earlier conversations.

Work out the user’s intent. After reading the prompt, the reviewer has to briefly describe what the user was trying to achieve with ChatGPT. Examples include answering a question, breaking down a complex topic, or editing a work message.

Analyze the AI’s responses. Next, the reviewer is shown four ChatGPT responses to the same prompt. They rate how well each response meets the established criteria, flag at least three strong or weak passages, and explain their score.

Rate. Each response is rated on a scale from 1 to 7, where 1 means the output is completely unacceptable and 7 means it can barely be improved upon. The score reflects not just how helpful and accurate the information is, but also tone, clarity, and how relevant it is to the user’s prompt.

Justify the score. Finally, the reviewer writes a brief explanation justifying the score. It can run anywhere from a couple of sentences to a full paragraph.

Importantly, people working on Project Lily can’t see the names or contact details in users’ ChatGPT profiles. But anyone who has ever chatted with AI can guess the catch: the prompts themselves often contain personal information that can reveal who the user is. The simplest example is a user who pastes their resume into an AI so it can proofread and polish it before it goes to a potential employer.

Before routing prompts to human reviewers, OpenAI runs them through a specialized AI model that is, in theory, supposed to strip out any information that can identify somebody. Even so, Project Lily reviewers say they often come across prompts that contain users’ personal data. OpenAI acknowledges that its anonymization model can make mistakes and miss certain personal details — particularly those details that are difficult to detect without broader context.

But where does OpenAI get these prompts from in the first place? For users on ChatGPT’s Free, Plus, and Pro tiers, OpenAI includes a setting that lets the company use their chats to improve its AI models. It’s enabled by default. This means the contents of those conversations can be used, among other things, for human review of ChatGPT’s responses. For Enterprise, Business, and Edu users, this setting is off by default, so their conversations aren’t used to improve AI models unless they give their permission.

If you’re on one of the other plans and you don’t want your conversations used to train and improve models, you need to disable this option yourself. The change applies only to new conversations and it’s not retroactive. At the end of this post, we’ll show you how to at least keep your future chats out of OpenAI’s grabby hands.

Who OpenAI trusts to review ChatGPT users’ prompts

404 Media was informed that a recruiting firm called Crossing Hurdles finds candidates and sends them to Mercor — the AI training company mentioned above. According to one worker, it’s Mercor that directly pays the contractors reviewing ChatGPT’s responses, offering a fairly generous rate of more than US$50 an hour.

In April of this year, another AI heavyweight — Meta — halted its business ties with Mercor after a large-scale data breach. The breach put at risk confidential AI training data that Mercor had prepared for its clients. At the time of publication of this blogpost, the full scope of the breach — and exactly what data ended up in the attackers’ hands — remained unclear. Meanwhile, OpenAI kept working with Mercor despite the Meta incident.

Human reviewers don’t just look at user chats to improve model quality, either. OpenAI may review conversations if its automated systems flag signs of potentially dangerous behavior — such as intent to harm others. These reviews are conducted for safety reasons, and are undertaken regardless of whether you allow your conversations to be used for AI model training. So even if you’ve turned that setting off, there’s no guarantee that a human will never see your conversations.

Who sees your nudes besides Copilot?

A few weeks after the Project Lily story, the same 404 Media reported on a similar practice over at Microsoft. The company has employees rate how accurately Copilot generates or edits images at users’ requests. And this report raises, arguably, even more questions about user privacy.

The employees who rate these images told 404 Media that they often have to deal with sexualized requests from users. For example, some requests ask to enlarge a woman’s breasts in a photo, shorten her skirt, or put a person in a sexualized pose.

And it’s not just AI-generated characters. These requests also involve photos of real people, who may have no idea their images are being uploaded to Copilot for this kind of manipulation. Most users likely don’t realize, either, that the images they generate or edit with AI can also be viewed by strangers.

Based on both the employees accounts and the documents the journalists reviewed, the image-rating process works roughly as follows:

Receive the user’s request. The reviewer gets both the original image uploaded to Copilot and the text instructions telling the AI how to edit it. For example, a user might ask to change how a person in a photo looks, or to add certain details.

Compare the AI’s outputs. Next, the reviewer gets two versions of the image that Copilot generated from the same request. Their job is to compare the results with each other and with the original photo.

Check against the request. The reviewer judges how closely the AI followed the user’s instructions. For example, if the user asked to change only one part of the image, the reviewer has to make sure everything else stayed untouched.

Look for visual flaws. Image quality is rated separately: the reviewer looks for distortions, unnatural details, and other visual artifacts introduced by processing.

Rate. Finally, the reviewer decides which of the two versions better fits the task, considering how accurately it follows the request, how well it keeps the original details, and image quality.

On paper, these steps may sound harmless enough. But reviewers themselves admit their job often boils down to judging whether an AI has made the breasts of the woman in the original image big enough. Furthermore, the images they review are not anonymized; the raw photos reveal people’s faces… as well as more intimate areas of their bodies.

The outlet also stresses that checking images for compliance with laws or platform rules isn’t part of the reviewers’ job. Some of the material they handle includes seriously disturbing requests — such as asking to undress girls who may be minors or to create images of animal sacrifice. Even so, the reviewers’ main task is to rate how accurately the AI carried out the user’s request — not to moderate that kind of content.

How can you protect your privacy when using chatbots?

As we’ve found out, conversations with AI, and the images you upload to chatbots, may be less private than many people expect. But can you do anything about it? ChatGPT users have more of a chance: they can opt out of having their data used to improve the models. With Copilot it’s more complicated.

When journalists asked about this, OpenAI representatives confirmed that the company uses ChatGPT users’ conversations to improve its AI models, and that includes having people review them. OpenAI stressed that before user prompts go to contractors, they’re automatically processed to remove personal data. However, the company admits that this process can’t always catch every scrap of information that could identify a user.

To stop OpenAI from using your data to improve and train its AI models, do the following in the web version:

Open Settings. To do this in the browser or Windows app, click your account in the bottom-left corner; on a Mac, find the matching item in the menu bar.

Click Data controls.

Turn off the toggle next to Improve the model for everyone.

In Settings → Data controls, turn off Improve the model for everyone so OpenAI doesn’t use your new conversations to train its models

Keep in mind that disabling this setting isn’t retroactive: conversations you had with ChatGPT before you switched it off may already have been used to train AI models. There’s no way to undo that, but you can at least stop your future conversations from being used for this purpose.

Now let’s move on to Copilot and Microsoft. When journalists reached out, Microsoft representatives said the company uses user data in line with its terms of service and privacy policy. In particular, this processing may be done to improve its products and enforce Copilot’s usage rules. However, Microsoft didn’t comment in detail on the practice the journalists described in which user images are sent to contractors for review.

As for opting out of having your data used to train AI, the situation here is a murkier. Older versions of Copilot had a dedicated setting that let users stop their conversations from being used to train models. But after an August 2026 update, the toggle disappeared from the interface, and Microsoft’s current documentation no longer has instructions for turning it off.

Microsoft claims that user prompts, Copilot responses, and the contents of uploaded files aren’t used to train foundation AI models. That doesn’t mean the company never uses this data to improve Copilot, though. So the only surefire way to keep Microsoft from showing your images to strangers to make Copilot better seems to be not to upload them at all.

Finally, one general tip. As the investigations we’ve covered in this post show, AI developers have very broad access to the data users share with chatbots. So it’s wise to assume by default that your chats with AI aren’t private, and to avoid including anything you wouldn’t want strangers to see.

What other privacy problems come with using AI, and how can you fix them? Find out in our other posts:

How AI tools are used for doxing

How to improve your resume with AI without exposing your data

Dear diary: how OpenAI’s Computer History feature works, and why it’s risky

Attacks on Gemini: the possibilities are endless

Unplugged: how to disable AI on your computer and smartphone

articles.title: Top corporate cyber-risks related to the human factor and social engineering
articles.context: A large share of breaches start with exploited vulnerabilities, but attacks that began with an employee mistake hold second place firmly
articles.full_text:
A large share of breaches start with exploited vulnerabilities, but attacks that began with an employee mistake hold second place firmly. Human risk keeps evolving along with the threat landscape, organizational change, and AI adoption in companies. To see what shifted most in 2026, the SANS Institute surveyed more than a thousand security professionals who specialize in human risk. And they’re nearly unanimous: social engineering attacks are getting more sophisticated and hitting more and more employees, and AI risks go well beyond employees sending data to public LLMs without approval.

Much of the report deals with the security job itself and its difficulties, but we focused on what matters most: what human-risk specialists see compared with what’s actually happening.

The misleading drop in password risk

Just 22% of respondents ranked weak passwords and weak authentication methods as their top risk – putting it in fourth place. Passwords have slid in this ranking for a second year running, creating the false impression that stricter password policies and mandatory multi-factor authentication (MFA) have improved things.

The reality is more complicated, and two factors matter most. First, part of the “password problem” now gets filed under social engineering. The report lumps everything into that category – from traditional phishing emails to deepfakes. But incident response data shows social engineering becoming more dangerous and more interactive. Employees are increasingly getting calls instead of messages supposedly from the help desk. Sometimes it’s the reverse: the attacker calls the corporate help desk and poses as an employee. Either way, the victim is pushed to reset MFA, read out a one-time code, or enroll a new MFA device, and the password is reset too if needed. The attackers end up controlling the account – having extracted both the password and the MFA. Treating this purely as a social-engineering problem is a mistake, and training rank-and-file employees alone won’t fix it.

Key here are extremely strict procedures for resetting both passwords and MFA – built into security policy. The right takeaway isn’t “we can forget about passwords” but “password policies should improve the way passwords are set”. Above all, the help desk needs training, including outsourced support teams. More on this below in the list of tips.

The second factor is the boom in infostealers. This type of malware steals secrets in bulk from infected computers and personal devices, giving attackers passwords of any length, MFA codes, or authentication tokens and cookies that bypass passwords entirely. That changes what employees need to know about passwords, but not how much it matters. Using unique passwords and keeping work passwords and sessions off personal devices as much as possible remain critical.

An ocean of AI risks

Risks linked to using AI at work have grown for the second year in a row – now firmly holding second place right behind social engineering. “Using AI” sounds simple, but the phrase hides a whole array of very different risks. Some are obvious, while some are easy to miss.

Shadow AI. The experts SANS surveyed say shadow AI is much bigger than shadow IT. More employees are involved, and they use a wider variety of unapproved tools at work. Vague messaging about using AI can add to the chaos. In many organizations, management pushes employees to be “AI-first” and to work more efficiently with AI, while the tools offered don’t suit the employees who have to use them, or managers give no specifics at all and just make demands. As a result employees rush to adopt AI tools they’re already familiar with or ones they’ve just found online. And they check with neither the security nor IT teams first.

Careless sharing of personal data or regulated or confidential information. This is the most obvious risk, and it keeps growing. No amount of training can beat the urge to get more done, and employees will still send confidential information to random AI tools. The only way to prevent incidents regarding confidential/personal data is to move to approved AI tools with built-in filters that strip personal data from inputs.

Weaker critical thinking and conflicts with security policies. This one is less obvious but still very dangerous. Many employees take AI output at face value without checking or questioning it. There are no exact statistics, but the rise of the slang term meat proxy suggests the problem is widespread. The habit of relying on AI means that when an employee hits an unclear IT or security situation, they turn to ChatGPT instead of company policy or a colleague who knows. Incidents related to poisoned AI answers show how dangerous this can be.

Vibe coding. Employees with no development background build internal tools, and sometimes external ones, on their own: dashboards, reports, process automation, and so on. They rely on AI and don’t check the output. The result is often a critically vulnerable application with access to important organizational data. SANS surveys show the practice has spread widely, and these freshly minted coders turn up in almost every department.

Departments that need extra attention

When it comes to how involved regular employees are in security, every department has people who support the process and people who resist it. The SANS report treats this mainly as a matter of office politics: it shows which departments are easier or harder to recruit as allies for security programs. But it also has a clear risk-forecasting angle. Departments in which employees are often targeted by phishing and social engineering, but where engagement with security programs is low, need extra attention from the SOC team. The usual holdouts are finance and operations. In finance, 17% of employees oppose security and 2% support it. In operations, it’s 23% against and 5% in favor. HR and external communications also push back quite a bit, with 13% and 12% opposed and 6% and 7% supportive. The report also lists middle and senior management as separate categories. Senior management is more likely to support security initiatives than obstruct them (21% and 17%, respectively). Middle managers, though, don’t want any security in 17% of cases, and support security initiatives in only 4%.

Tech support staff (service desk, IT support, and similar roles) are a key target of modern social engineering attacks. The statistics don’t list them separately, but, overall, only 10% of IT employees are against security processes, while 28% support them.

How to reduce human risk in 2026

We’ve split the tips below into several sections, each aimed at a different group of employees. For many of these tips, training alone isn’t enough. It’s also essential to update a company’s security policies. Set up approved, filtered access to AI, assign clear responsibility for rolling out AI agents, and formalize how to verify someone’s identity when they ask for a password or MFA reset.

To make training stick instead of staying theoretical, add game mechanics, cyber drills, and repetition – adapted to how fast each person learns. Specialized platforms such as aspersky Automated Security Awareness Platform help roll this out across the whole organization.

What to teach all employees

If anyone contacts you by phone, text, or messaging app, and asks you to share or reset your password or MFA code, or confirm an action – end the conversation. Then contact the company help desk through a channel you already know – even if the caller’s number looks familiar.

No one – not even the IT department – will ever ask for your password or MFA code.

Never approve an MFA request if you didn’t start the sign-in process yourself.

Never paste or run technical commands in the Start menu search bar, Run window, or any other command line if a website, CAPTCHA window, or pop-up message tells you to.

Install software only from approved, official sources. Don’t use cracked software or game mods on devices you use for work.

The same goes for browser extensions. Use only well-known extensions that IT and security teams have approved.

Don’t sign in to work accounts or sync your work browser profile on personal devices.

Use a password manager, and a unique password for every account. Never reuse the same password for work and personal accounts.

Use only approved AI tools, and keep in mind which tool is meant for which type of information. A tool may be approved for business correspondence, for example, but banned for processing customer data.

Never enter customer data or confidential or internal information into public AI services.

Check AI output before you use it. You’re the one responsible for the result.

AI recommendations never override security requirements. If the two seem to contradict each other, call the security team or the help desk and ask for advice.

Don’t use apps, scripts, or agents created with AI at work without sign-off from both management and the security staff responsible for AI deployments.

Report suspicious events – such as strange emails and calls – even if you think you handled them well yourself. These reports can help stop an attack on your coworkers.

What to teach specific groups of employees

User support and IT help desks (including outside contractors)

Never reset a password or MFA during an incoming call. Always call the employee back at the number in the company directory.

Verify an employee’s identity on a video call where they show an ID document. Personal details or a manager’s name given over the phone aren’t enough – since attackers often already have this information.

Before any MFA change or administrator account reset, get confirmation from the employee’s manager through a separate channel. If something seems off, require the employee to show up in person.

If a caller claims to be a vendor employee and asks for access, end the call, then contact the vendor’s account manager using the contact details in the contract with the vendor.

Treat urgency, a caller’s senior job title, or contact outside working hours as warning signs of an attack.

Don’t accept work instructions from colleagues through text messages or other channels not meant for work.

Finance teams, executives, and their assistants

Confirm every payment, change of bank details, or access request by calling back on a number you already know. Do this even if the request came by voice or video call.

Attackers can create voice and video deepfakes of your boss or other managers. Agree in advance with your boss on a few ways to check suspicious requests, such as calling back on a different line or using a code word.

Developers and anyone who builds software with AI (vibe coding)

Review AI-generated code as carefully as you would an intern’s work. If you don’t have the skills to do that, ask colleagues who do.

Never put secrets, keys, or credentials in code or in prompts to AI.

Remember: if you create an AI agent, you’re responsible for what it does. Give it only the minimum permissions it needs, and require human approval for any action that can’t be undone.

For more detailed tips on safe vibe coding, see our separate post.

What to change in your security awareness programs

Drop password complexity rules and regular password changes from your training. Instead, teach people to use unique long passwords and to store them in password managers.

Add simulated attacks to your program – such as voice phishing (vishing) and fake CAPTCHA windows. Include attacks aimed at the help desk.

Never shame employees who fail a simulated attack. Help them understand their mistakes and build confidence instead.

Replace one big annual awareness course with short, regular training sessions. Base them on real incidents and on where your company currently stands on AI adoption.

Run role-specific training for the help desk, finance team, executives, and developers.

Let people report an incident with just one click or call, and publicly thank those who do.

Track the reporting rate for suspicious events and also the time to report, rather than the phishing click rate.

articles.title: Black Friday, red flags: too-good-to-be-true deals hiding real threats
articles.context: Despite differing mechanics, both approaches exploit the same vulnerability – reflexive trust in a familiar brand whose identity the scammers have appropriated – and simply...
articles.full_text:
Intro

Black Friday remains a defining moment of the holiday shopping season and a key period for cybercriminals seeking to exploit the surge in consumer activity. The scale of this demand is reflected in seasonal spending patterns. According to PwC’s post-holiday analysis, holiday spending rose by 6.4% year over year in 2025, with Black Friday once again being the peak sales day generating nearly $20 billion. Consumer behavior points to the same trend: KPMG’s 2026 Consumer Pulse Survey found that Black Friday remains the most important sales event, with 62% of respondents pointing to its importance. Moreover, it is strongly associated with online shopping, with 83% of consumers preferring to buy online or combine online and in-person purchases on this occasion. To find the best offers, 55% of respondents in 2026 planned to research purchases through retailer websites and 46% through brand websites. As shopping activity concentrates online during peak sales periods, threat actors gain broader opportunities to exploit consumer demand, trusted brands, and heavy promotional traffic to steal credentials, payment data, and money.

At Kaspersky, we closely follow the cybersecurity risks associated with major shopping events and seasonal spikes in online retail activity. Our annual analysis examines how cybercriminals adapt their tactics to target consumers during high-demand sales periods.

This report extends our annual Securelist series published in 2021, 2022, 2023, 2024, and 2025, exploring how shopping-related cyberthreats continue to evolve.

Methodology

To keep pace with the evolving shopping threat landscape, we conduct an annual assessment of the most prevalent malicious techniques, including financial malware, phishing pages impersonating major retailers, e-commerce platforms, digital services, banks, and payment providers, as well as spam campaigns designed to steer users to fraudulent sites. The threat data we rely on is sourced from Kaspersky Security Network (KSN), which processes anonymized cybersecurity data shared consensually by Kaspersky users.

Most of the data in this report draws on was collected from January through October 2026.

Key findings

In the first ten months of 2026, Kaspersky identified more than 19 million phishing attacks targeting users of online stores, payment systems and banks, a year-on-year increase of 1%.

As many as 5% of these attacks were directed at online shoppers.

Around 84% of all phishing attacks targeting users of online stores and subscription services involve scammers impersonating Amazon, Apple, Netflix, Shopify and Alibaba Group pages.

Netflix-themed phishing detections grew by 5% in 2026 in comparison with 2025 data.

We detected more than 220,071 sales-themed spam messages in the first two weeks of November, which is 50.2% more than in 2025.

More than 801,000 banking Trojan attacks were recorded during the first 10 months of 2026.

Between June and November 2026, Kaspersky products have already detected over 27,000 attacks by malware and potentially unwanted applications posing as GTA VI-related content.

Shopping-related phishing by the numbers

Phishing and scams remain among the most persistent threats for online shoppers, particularly during peak sales periods, when heightened transaction volumes and time-sensitive offers create conditions for abuse. One of the most notable developments in recent years has been the growing use of AI to increase the speed, scale and sophistication of such campaigns. AI-enabled tools can be used to generate convincing phishing emails, fraudulent shopping pages, and realistic seller identities, while also adapting messages and visuals to mimic legitimate brands. In the context of major retail events, where consumers often move quickly across marketplaces, social platforms, and promotional channels, this added level of automation further increases the risk of deception, credential theft, and financial loss.

Although phishing has long remained a common method of deceiving users, we are seeing a growing number of attacks in segments related to online shopping. From January through October 2026, Kaspersky products blocked 19,063,077 attempts to access phishing links targeting users of online stores, payment systems, and banks – nearly three times (198.1%) more than during the same period last year, when 6,394,854 such attempts were recorded. A breakdown of these attempts shows that 44.54% targeted online shoppers, compared with 48.21% in 2025; 28.55% targeted banking users, up from 26.10%; and 26.91% mimicked payment systems, versus 25.69% last year.

Financial phishing attacks by category, January–October 2026 (download)

Since 2021, we have conducted annual assessments of the distribution of phishing attacks targeting users across popular online platforms, including Amazon, Alibaba Group, eBay, Mercado Libre, and Walmart, in order to track how the attackers abuse trusted brands. In 2026, Kaspersky products detected and blocked 3,102,304 phishing attempts involving the misuse of Amazon’s brand, up 411.6% from 606,369 attempts in 2025. Threat actors consistently stick to leveraging well-known and trusted consumer platforms to enhance the credibility of fraudulent pages.

Other major e-commerce brands were also widely impersonated in phishing campaigns. Kaspersky detected 360,949 attempts to visit phishing pages mimicking Alibaba-owned brands including AliExpress, while eBay-themed phishing pages accounted for 163,381 alerts. The Latin American marketplace Mercado Libre was used as a lure in 109,081 cases, and Walmart-related phishing pages were identified 74,220 times.

Popular online stores mimicked by scammers, January–October 2026 (download)

The rankings of platforms most frequently impersonated by scammers include more than just brands directly associated with tangible items. The attackers are equally interested in scamming users of popular services selling digital products, such as music, TV shows, e-books, and others. The overall top five brands abused in 2026 were Amazon, Apple, Netflix, Shopify, and Alibaba Group–associated brands, which together were mimicked in 7,119,400 detections. Overall, these five platforms represented 83.83% of all phishing attacks associated with online stores and subscription services.

TOP 5 online platforms mimicked by scammers, January–October 2026 (download)

As mentioned before, Amazon was abused in 3,102,304 detections, or 36.53% of the total. Phishing pages impersonating Apple-related resources accounted for 1,622,917 detections, or 19.1%. Netflix-themed phishing accounted for 1,365,648 detections, or 16.08% of the total, marking a 70.5% increase from 801,148 detections recorded in 2025. Shopify-themed phishing accounted for 667,582 detections, or 7.86%.

What mass scam campaigns look like

Mass scam campaigns often rely on phishing kits or templates that can be used to quickly build numerous pages that target different markets, languages, and user segments and mimic widely used platforms. These platforms are broadly recognized and generally trusted by the users, while standardized scam flows allow attackers to scale operations with minimal effort. Across these campaigns, scammers combine familiar visual design, urgent calls to action, and fake login, payment, or verification pages.

Brand recognition in this scenario works against users: the more familiar an interface looks, the less likely a visitor is to question its authenticity. This logic forms the basis of a whole cluster of phishing campaigns that abuse the names of major tech platforms. Fraudulent pages copying login pages of these platforms reproduce the original layout, branding, and even alternative sign-in options, leaving credential entry forms as the only interactive element – everything typed into these forms goes straight to the attackers. Hijacked logins to an e-commerce platform potentially open the door not only to the victims’ purchase history or payment methods in this exact store, but also to other accounts that use the same login credentials.

Scammers often create pages that replicate the fonts and visual style of the original site. This example mimics an Amazon page

A common technique for stealing login credentials. Example of a fake website impersonating Shopify

A related but noisier approach relies on manufactured urgency: we detected pages masquerading as Apple support that bombard the visitor with alarming pop-ups about a suspicious Apple Pay “pre-authorization” and urge them to immediately call a “support number”. If the user contacts the phone number, fake operators will try to talk the victim into revealing sensitive details or granting remote access to their device, which can be used to steal money and data. Despite differing mechanics, both approaches exploit the same vulnerability – reflexive trust in a familiar brand whose identity the scammers have appropriated – and simply choose different triggers: routine in the first case, panic in the second.

Example of a scam page exploiting a sense of urgency

There’s usually a variety of scams abusing users’ trust and the hype surrounding Apple devices. Fake stores appearing to sell or lease iPhones for “low monthly payments” are one example of such scams.

Scammers consistently target fans of flagship smartphones. Example of a fake page impersonating Apple

The streaming platform discount trap

Black Friday has become a major subscriber acquisition window for subscription-based streaming services rather than a peripheral promotional event. Antenna estimates that Black Friday drove 8.9 million incremental premium subscription video-on-demand (SVOD) sign-ups in 2025 and accounted for roughly 25% of all November sign-ups, an 800,000 increase compared to 2024, when Black Friday promotions generated 8.1 million sign-ups.

This concentration of promotional activity also expands the space for abuse. As subscription platforms compete for user attention with discounts, limited-time offers, and account-based promotions, threat actors can easily repurpose the same themes across phishing pages and fraudulent payment forms. In this context, brands tied to subscriptions, billing, account access, and merchant services are used as lures: they are widely recognized, naturally associated with recurring payments and promotional offers and therefore likely to prompt user engagement.

Netflix remained among the top five online-store and subscription-service brands most frequently abused by scammers, highlighting the persistent use of streaming services as lures in brand-abuse campaigns. While the majority of observed schemes affecting this platform simply sought to phish users’ credentials, we also saw “generous offers” trying to lure users with discounts. In one example, the attackers embedded the Netflix name in a bundle with other services, such as telecom or entertainment packages. The fraudulent page is designed to collect a range of personal data. Afterwards, the attackers contact the victim via WhatsApp to ask for further information or money. Another scheme imitates the platform itself, offering fake discounted subscription deals. In both scenarios, attackers exploit trust in a globally recognized entertainment brand to increase engagement and push users toward sharing sensitive details or paying money.

Scammers create Netflix-themed fake pages to harvest personal and payment data or sell nonexistent subscriptions

Subscription entertainment brands, such as Spotify and YouTube Premium, are also being used as phishing lures to collect either payment card data through fake subscription forms or account credentials through counterfeit login pages. Informal “support” channels, such as WhatsApp chats, add credibility and help attackers guide victims in real time.

Subscription-service scams impersonate Spotify and YouTube Premium to steal payment details and account credentials

Inside the Black Friday spam wave targeting shoppers

In 2026, Black Friday–related scams continued to spread across multiple channels, with fraudulent email campaigns remaining one of the ways they reached their victims. As retailers stepped up their seasonal marketing, cybercriminals took advantage of the flood of promotional messages by sending look-alike emails. During the first two weeks of November, Kaspersky detected 220,071 spam messages related to the sales season – 50,18% more than in 2025. Over the same period, 1,728 of the identified spam messages referenced Singles’ Day promotions in Asia.

Scam campaigns built around Apple products begin long before Black Friday: fraudulent activity traditionally spikes on the eve of Apple’s keynotes and then flows seamlessly into the November sales season. In one example, a link from a spam email leads to a fake store impersonating a telecom operator, which offers the new iPhone 18 Pro Max at a tiny fraction of its retail price as a “time-limited special offer”.

An example of a detected spam email impersonating a Telenor marketing proposal. The email offers a new smartphone model for sale

The page mimics the real provider’s product page and is most likely designed to trick the user into entering payment card details.

Scammers created a fake page impersonating the Telenor online store. The users land on the website through a link in a spam email

Alongside fake stores, gamified giveaways are still a persistent email scam format of the sales season: instead of simply offering a discount, fraudsters invite users to “win” a prize, which makes users lower their guard and adds an element of excitement. Pages of this kind typically impersonate well-known retail brands and use personalized greetings, limited attempts, and guaranteed “wins” to create an impression of an exclusive, harmless lottery. The prize, of course, is predetermined and serves only as a pretext to request personal and payment card details, allegedly to cover delivery. Exploiting trust in household retail names, such schemes leave victims with compromised card data or stolen money instead of a gift.

Fake REWE-branded Black Friday giveaway offering a free gift for guessing a “secret number”

Wasted: GTA VI “offers” and other lures targeting the gaming community this November

In November 2026, the gaming industry is set for one of its most anticipated launches in years: GTA VI. Highly awaited game releases have long created openings for cybercriminal activity. In our 2024 Kaspersky Security Bulletin, we predicted that cybercriminals would seek to exploit GTA VI’s popularity. In fact, the risk is also amplified by timing: the game’s November 19 launch coincides with the seasonal sales campaigns, when users are already primed to look for discounts, bundles, and limited-time offers. This means users need to be extra cautious.

Malware campaigns typically cluster around the game itself, using the surrounding attention to disguise malicious files as related content; between June and November 2026, Kaspersky detected 27,416 malware and potentially unwanted application attacks posing as GTA VI–related content. At the same time, phishing schemes follow a separate logic: they exploit purchase intent and urgency around offers, driving users to fake pages.

In the example below, a fake store offers Brazilian users a chance to buy a PS5 subscription bundle with GTA VI included. Scammers offer payment options via a banking card or Pix. If the user pays, they never see either PlayStation or the game.

Besides GTA VI, all traditional gaming phishing and scam schemes are also present. The screenshot below shows a fraudulent website mimicking Steam that allegedly gives away $50 gift cards as part of a “Winter Gift Marathon”. To get the card, users are urged to log in to their Steam accounts, compromising their credentials.

Another scheme invites users to a Discord group chat. However, when the victim tries to enter the chat, a pop-up window appears telling them that they need to install a security module. If they click the “Install” button, a suspicious file is downloaded to their device.

From self-care to scam: how attackers target beauty and wellness fans

In addition to shopping-related scams, cybercriminals have continued to exploit consumer interest in personal health, wellness, and beauty in 2026. These themes have long been present in spam and phishing activity, as they combine broad consumer appeal with topics that often involve sensitive personal decisions and data. The continued expansion of online health services, consultations, and wellness products also makes such lures appear more familiar and plausible to users.

Weight loss was one of the health-related themes observed in spam campaigns. In one identified example, a link in a spam email redirected the recipient to a page promoting a telehealth weight-loss service. The page used likely fabricated credibility markers – such as claims of “1,000s of patients” and “600+ doctors” – to make the site appear as an established medical provider. The prompt to “qualify in 5 minutes” through an online assessment acted as the first step in the conversion funnel. Depending on the scheme, such websites may further prompt users to enter their personal and medical data into a fraudulent form, may steal money, or just sell dubious products or services under the guise of a magic pill.

An example of a weight-loss telehealth page

Another spam email targeted users concerned about skin aging. It used a health-advisory style banner and a clickbait headline presenting “The 1 Vitamin You Need if You Have Wrinkled Skin” as a dermatologist’s recommendation. By combining appeals to medical authority and social proof, such as mentioning thousands who already use this vitamin, and framing the offer as free advice through the call to action “Tap For Recipe,” the campaign lowered users’ guard.

A spam email banner promoting a dubious anti-aging supplement through fake dermatologist claims

The link from the email redirects users to a fraudulent site that imitates a legitimate skincare brand and uses a sensational headline about a “$1 Japanese pink vitamin” allegedly responsible for a famous actress’s youthful appearance – a claim the celebrity never made. A fabricated comment section showing more than 36,000 “comments” creates fake social proof and guides visitors toward purchasing a dubious supplement (if it exists at all).

A fraudulent skincare-themed page using a fake celebrity endorsement

Beauty-themed scams are distributed not only by email. Moreover, they are not limited to miracle supplements; fraudsters also exploit the appeal of luxury cosmetics offered at implausibly low prices. In the example below, a fake online store impersonates a trusted retailer, Sephora, and advertises branded perfume at a fraction of its retail price. The page combines familiar pressure tactics, including a fabricated rating, a scarcity warning (“only 6 bottles left”), a one-bottle-per-customer limit and a countdown timer. Together, these elements are designed to rush victims into paying for products that will never be delivered.

Example of a fake beauty retailer page encouraging users to make a purchase on sale

Banking Trojans

Banking Trojans remained active in 2026. On PC, they can monitor browser activity, inject fraudulent content into legitimate sessions, intercept credentials and card data, and in some cases, manipulate payment details or cryptocurrency transactions. On mobile devices, they usually target a range of banking and online store apps, using various techniques to obtain user credentials or interfere with transactions. This makes banking Trojans particularly dangerous around major retail sales, when fast purchase decisions and intensified use of digital payment flows increase the risk of financial theft.

PC banker activity continued to decline year over year: in the first ten months of 2026, Kaspersky detected 801,150* attacks, compared with more than 1.09 million in 2025. This trend persists due to the continuous shift away from PC bankers toward mobile-first fraud and credential theft. Even so, PC banking malware remained active throughout the year. One example is GoPix, a Brazilian banking Trojan delivered through Google Ads malvertising and designed to abuse Pix, Boleto and cryptocurrency transactions. Other noteworthy threats are JanelaRAT, which targeted online banking users in Brazil and Mexico, and Horabot, which continued to surface in multistage campaigns combining banking malware with email-based propagation.

In the mobile segment, BeatBanker is worth mentioning: an Android banker active in Brazil, distributed via a fake Google Play page and bundled with a crypto miner.

*These statistics include globally active banking malware, and malware for ATMs and point-of-sale (PoS) systems. We excluded data on Trojan banker families that no longer use banking Trojan functionality in their attacks, such as Emotet.

Conclusions

Kaspersky’s phishing data points to a rise in shopping-related threats: from January to October 2026, phishing attempts targeting users of online stores, payment systems and banks increased by 198.1% compared with the same period in 2025. The main tactic remained brand impersonation: scammers abused the names of major online platforms and digital services to create fake login pages, payment forms, support alerts, and subscription offers. Amazon-themed phishing grew by 411.6% year over year, while detections of fraudulent pages abusing Netflix increased by 70.5%.

Black Friday-themed spam also intensified, rising by 50.2% compared with 2025. These campaigns blended into the broader flow of seasonal promotions and redirected users to fraudulent websites. Beyond traditional retail, attackers used lures tied to subscriptions, gaming, and health and wellness, showing how scams are adjusted to current consumer interests. Banking Trojans remained active, although PC banker detections declined year over year, as attackers continued shifting from traditional desktop banking malware toward mobile-first scenarios.

Overall, the findings show that major shopping periods remain associated with a higher concentration of recurring cyberthreats. During seasonal sales events, users should be especially cautious with unsolicited offers, verify websites before entering data, and treat unusually generous discounts or urgent requests with skepticism. To make sure that they don’t end up on a fraudulent website amid the shopping rush, we recommend that users protect their devices with a comprehensive security solution, such as Kaspersky Premium, which uses an advanced AI-powered detection technology that analyzes website characteristics and URLs to identify suspicious patterns. In 2026, Kaspersky Premium was awarded an “Approved” certificate by AV-Comparatives for the second year in a row for its ability to detect fake online stores.

articles.title: How to protect a company from attacks through AI agents | Kaspersky official blog
